questions.explanation: Shop A: sum 75, mean 15, range 20 − 10 = 10. Shop B: sum 75, mean 15, range 17 − 13 = 4. The means are equal, but Shop A's sales are more varied.

questions.q: Sara recorded the number of books she read each month. Year 1: 5, 9, 7, 6, 8. Year 2: 2, 14, 10, 4, 15. Which statement is correct?
options: Year 1 has the greater mean, and Year 2 is more varied.
Year 2 has the greater mean and is more varied.
Year 1 has the greater mean and is more varied.
Year 2 has the greater mean, and Year 1 is more varied.
questions.hint: Find both means and both ranges.
questions.explanation: Year 1: sum 35, mean 7, range 9 − 5 = 4. Year 2: sum 45, mean 9, range 15 − 2 = 13. Year 2 has the greater mean and is more varied.

questions.q: Quiz scores (out of 10). Class A: 8, 9, 7, 10, 9, 8, 9, 8. Class B: 10, 5, 9, 10, 6, 10, 4, 8. Which statement is correct?
options: Class A has the higher average and is more varied.
Class A has the higher average, and Class B is more varied.
Class B has the higher average and is more varied.
Class B has the higher average, and Class A is more varied.
questions.hint: Find the mean and range of each class.
questions.explanation: Class A: sum 68, mean 8.5, range 10 − 7 = 3. Class B: sum 62, mean 7.75, range 10 − 4 = 6. Class A has the higher average and Class B is more varied.

questions.q: Test scores. Class C: 12, 15, 18, 15, 20. Class D: 16, 17, 15, 16, 16. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Mean = sum ÷ number of scores.
questions.explanation: Class C: sum 80, mean 16, range 20 − 12 = 8. Class D: sum 80, mean 16, range 17 − 15 = 2. Both have the same mean, but Class C is more varied.

questions.q: Points scored in four games. Red team: 14, 18, 16, 20. Blue team: 19, 21, 18, 22. Write Red or Blue.
questions.hint: Compare the means, then the ranges.
questions.explanation: Red: sum 68, mean 17, range 6. Blue: sum 80, mean 20, range 4. Blue has the higher average, but Red's scores are more varied.

questions.q: Set 1: 5, 7, 6, 8, 4. Set 2: 2, 12, 9, 3, 9. Which statement correctly describes the data?
options: Set 2 has a greater mean and is more varied.
Set 1 has a greater mean and is more varied.
Set 1 has a greater mean and Set 2 is more varied.
Set 1 is more varied and Set 2 has a greater mean.
questions.hint: Compute each mean and range.
questions.explanation: Set 1: sum 30, mean 6, range 8 − 4 = 4. Set 2: sum 35, mean 7, range 12 − 2 = 10. Set 2 has the greater mean and is more varied.

questions.q: Complete the table for the three data sets. Set A: 3, 9, 6, 6, 6. Set B: 1, 11, 4, 8, 6. Set C: 5, 7, 6, 6, 6.
questions.hint: Each set has 5 values; the range is greatest minus least.
questions.explanation: Each set sums to 30, so every mean is 6. The ranges are 9 − 3 = 6, 11 − 1 = 10 and 7 − 5 = 2, so Set B is the most varied and Set C the least.

questions.hint: Find the mean and range of each set.
questions.explanation: Set X: sum 120, mean 24, range 8. Set Y: sum 125, mean 25, range 40 − 10 = 30. Set Y has the greater mean and is more varied.

questions.q: Goals scored in 8 matches. Team X: 3, 4, 2, 5, 4, 3, 4, 3. Team Y: 1, 6, 0, 7, 2, 5, 1, 2. Which statement correctly describes the data?
options: On average Team X scored more, and Team X's goals were more varied.
On average Team X scored more, but Team Y's goals were more varied.
On average Team Y scored more, and Team Y's goals were more varied.
On average Team Y scored more, but Team X's goals were more varied.
questions.hint: Find the mean and range for each team.
questions.explanation: Team X: sum 28, mean 3.5, range 5 − 2 = 3. Team Y: sum 24, mean 3, range 7 − 0 = 7. Team X has the higher mean and Team Y is more varied.

questions.q: For the data 6, 9, 12, 20, 23, match each statistic with its value.
questions.hint: Order the data first to find the median.
questions.explanation: The sum is 70, so the mean is 70 ÷ 5 = 14. The middle value of 6, 9, 12, 20, 23 is 12. The range is 23 − 6 = 17.

questions.q: Daily visitors over 5 days. Store P: 50, 52, 48, 51, 49. Store Q: 30, 70, 45, 65, 40. Complete:
questions.hint: Two sets can have the same mean but very different spreads.
questions.explanation: Store P: sum 250, mean 50, range 4. Store Q: sum 250, mean 50, range 70 − 30 = 40. The means are equal, but Store Q's numbers are far more varied.

questions.q: Classify each random variable as discrete or continuous.

left: The number of cars in a parking lot
The time taken to run 100 m
The number of goals in a football match

questions.hint: Counted quantities are discrete; measured quantities are continuous.
questions.explanation: Cars and goals are counted in whole numbers, so they are discrete. Time, mass and temperature are measured and can take any value in an interval, so they are continuous.

questions.q: Which random variable is discrete?
options: The number of students absent today
The volume of water in a tank
The time to finish a test
questions.hint: Look for something you count rather than measure.
questions.explanation: The number of absent students is counted (0, 1, 2, …), so it is discrete. Height, volume and time are measured, so they are continuous.

questions.q: Which random variable is continuous?
options: The amount of petrol (in litres) in a car's tank
The number of heads in 10 coin tosses
The number of text messages sent in a day
The number of siblings a student has
questions.hint: Continuous variables are measured and can take any value in a range.
questions.explanation: Petrol in litres can be any value such as 23.48 L, so it is continuous. The other three are counts, so they are discrete.

questions.q: Complete the table by writing discrete or continuous.

rows: Number of books on a shelf
Number of customers in an hour

questions.hint: Ask yourself: is it counted or measured?
questions.explanation: Books and customers are counted, so they are discrete. The length of a call and a baby's weight are measured, so they are continuous.

questions.q: In a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ, match each region with the percent of data it contains.
questions.hint: Split 68%, 95% and 99.7% in half and take differences.

questions.q: In a normal distribution, about what percent of the data lies between μ − 2σ and μ + 2σ?
questions.hint: Use the 68–95–99.7 rule.
questions.explanation: By the empirical rule, about 68% lies within 1 standard deviation, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3. So the answer is 95%.

questions.q: Complete the table for a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ.
questions.hint: The region from μ to μ + 2σ is half of the middle 95%.
questions.explanation: The empirical rule gives 68%, 95% and 99.7% for 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations. From μ to μ + 2σ is half of 95%, which is 47.5%.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 6. Complete:
questions.hint: Count how many standard deviations each endpoint is from the mean.
questions.explanation: 34 and 46 are 1 standard deviation from 40 (40 ± 6), giving 68%. 28 and 52 are 2 standard deviations away (40 ± 12), giving 95%. 22 and 58 are 3 standard deviations away (40 ± 18), giving 99.7%.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 8. Which range represents the middle 95%?
questions.hint: The middle 95% is within 2 standard deviations of the mean.
questions.explanation: 2 standard deviations = 2 × 8 = 16. 70 − 16 = 54 and 70 + 16 = 86, so the middle 95% is 54 < X < 86.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Match each range with the percent of data it contains.
questions.hint: Write each endpoint as the mean plus or minus a number of standard deviations.
questions.explanation: 100 ± 15 covers 68%, 100 ± 30 covers 95%, and 100 ± 45 covers 99.7%. From the mean up to 1 standard deviation above (100 to 115) is half of 68%, which is 34%.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 62.5 and a standard deviation of 4.25. Use the empirical rule to find the range of values that represents the middle 95%. Write it as a < X < b.
questions.hint: The middle 95% is within 2 standard deviations of the mean.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 120 and a standard deviation of 7.5. Which range represents the middle 68%?
questions.hint: The middle 68% is within 1 standard deviation of the mean.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 35.6 and a standard deviation of 2.8. Find the range of values that represents the middle 99.7%.
questions.hint: The middle 99.7% is within 3 standard deviations of the mean.

questions.q: What is the value of z if X = 31, μ = 19 and σ = 4?
questions.hint: Use z = (X − μ) / σ.

questions.q: A normal distribution has μ = 50 and σ = 5. Complete the table of z-scores.
Find the z-score of X = 12.4 if μ = 15 and σ = 1.3.
questions.hint: Subtract the mean first, then divide by the standard deviation.
questions.explanation: z = (12.4 − 15) / 1.3 = −2.6 / 1.3 = −2. The value is 2 standard deviations below the mean.

questions.q: What is the value of X if μ = 20, σ = 4 and the z-score of X is z = 2.25?
questions.hint: Rearrange z = (X − μ)/σ to X = μ + zσ.

questions.q: What is the value of X if μ = 65, σ = 5 and z = −1.8?
questions.hint: Use X = μ + zσ and keep the negative sign.

questions.q: A normal distribution has μ = 12 and σ = 2.5. Complete the table.
A normal distribution has a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 3. Write True or False for each statement.

rows: 84% of the data is less than 43.
95% of the data is between 31 and 49.
13.5% of the data is between 43 and 46.
2.5% of the data is greater than 46.
50% of the data is between 40 and 49.

questions.hint: Write each number as the mean plus or minus some standard deviations.
questions.explanation: 43 is +1σ, so 50% + 34% = 84% is below it (true). 31 and 49 are ±3σ, which is 99.7%, not 95% (false). 43 to 46 is +1σ to +2σ, which is 13.5% (true). Above 46 (+2σ) is 2.5% (true). 40 to 49 is 0 to +3σ, which is 49.85%, not 50% (false).

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 20 and a standard deviation of 2.5. Which statement is true?
options: 68% of the data is between 15 and 25.
2.5% of the data is less than 12.5.
95% of the data is between 17.5 and 22.5.
16% of the data is greater than 22.5.
questions.hint: Find how many standard deviations each value is from 20.
questions.explanation: 22.5 is +1σ, and 50% − 34% = 16% lies above it, so the first statement is true. 17.5 to 22.5 is ±1σ (68%), 12.5 is −3σ (0.15% below), and 15 to 25 is ±2σ (95%), so the other statements are false.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 80 and a standard deviation of 6. Complete with percents.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Percent of data less than 62 or greater than 98:

questions.hint: 86 is +1σ, 68 and 74 are −2σ and −1σ, and 62 and 98 are ±3σ.
questions.explanation: Below +1σ is 50% + 34% = 84%. Between −2σ and −1σ is 13.5%. Outside ±3σ is 100% − 99.7% = 0.3%.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 45.5 and a standard deviation of 2.5. What percent of the data will be greater than 48?
questions.hint: Find the z-score of 48 first.
questions.explanation: z = (48 − 45.5)/2.5 = 1. Above 1 standard deviation is 50% − 34% = 16%.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 120 and a standard deviation of 10. What percent of the data will be greater than 90?
questions.hint: 90 is below the mean, so most of the data is greater than it.
questions.explanation: z = (90 − 120)/10 = −3. Between −3σ and the mean is 49.85%, and above the mean is 50%, so 49.85% + 50% = 99.85% is greater than 90.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 30 and a standard deviation of 4. Complete the table with the percent of data greater than each value.
questions.hint: Turn each X into a number of standard deviations from 30.
questions.explanation: 34 is +1σ, so 16% is above. 38 is +2σ, so 2.5% is above. 42 is +3σ, so 0.15% is above. 26 is −1σ, so 34% + 50% = 84% is above.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 22.4 and a standard deviation of 1.8. What percent of the data will be less than 17?
questions.explanation: z = −5.4/1.8 = −3. Below 3 standard deviations under the mean is (100% − 99.7%)/2 = 0.15%.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 64 and a standard deviation of 7. What percent of the data will be less than 71?
questions.hint: 71 is one standard deviation above the mean.
questions.explanation: z = (71 − 64)/7 = 1. Below the mean is 50% and between the mean and +1σ is 34%, so 84% of the data is less than 71.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 9.6 and a standard deviation of 0.8. Complete:
questions.hint: Find the z-score, then use the empirical rule for the lower tail.
questions.explanation: z = (8.0 − 9.6)/0.8 = −1.6/0.8 = −2. 95% lies within 2 standard deviations, leaving 5% in the two tails, so 2.5% is below 8.0.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 48 and a standard deviation of 6. Find the range of values that represents the middle 68% of the distribution.
questions.hint: The middle 68% is within 1 standard deviation of the mean.
questions.explanation: 48 − 6 = 42 and 48 + 6 = 54, so the middle 68% is 42 < x < 54.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 15.5 and a standard deviation of 1.5. Find the range of values for the middle 68%.
questions.hint: Subtract and add one standard deviation.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 200 and a standard deviation of 20. Match each middle percent with its range.
questions.hint: 68%, 95% and 99.7% go with 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 24 and a standard deviation of 3. What percent of the data will be greater than 30?
questions.hint: Find how many standard deviations 30 is above 24.
questions.explanation: z = (30 − 24)/3 = 2. 95% lies within 2 standard deviations, leaving 5% in the two tails, so 2.5% is greater than 30.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 7 and a standard deviation of 1.5. What percent of the data will be greater than 11.5?
questions.explanation: z = 4.5/1.5 = 3. 99.7% lies within 3 standard deviations, leaving 0.3% in the two tails, so 0.15% is above 11.5.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 4. Complete the table with the percent of data less than each value.
questions.hint: Find each value's distance from 50 in standard deviations.
questions.explanation: 54 is +1σ, so 84% is below. 42 is −2σ, so 2.5% is below. 38 is −3σ, so 0.15% is below. 50 is the mean, so 50% is below.

questions.q: Heights of students are normally distributed with a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 6 cm. What percent of students are between 158 cm and 176 cm tall?
questions.hint: Find the z-scores of both heights, then add the regions between them.
questions.explanation: z(158) = (158 − 170)/6 = −2 and z(176) = (176 − 170)/6 = 1. From −2σ to the mean is 47.5% and from the mean to +1σ is 34%, so the total is 81.5%.

questions.q: Exam scores are normally distributed with a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 40. What percent of scores are between 380 and 540?
questions.hint: 380 is 3 standard deviations below the mean; 540 is 1 above.
questions.explanation: z(380) = −120/40 = −3 and z(540) = 40/40 = 1. From −3σ to the mean is 49.85% and from the mean to +1σ is 34%, so the total is 83.85%.

questions.q: Weights of parcels are normally distributed with a mean of 75 kg and a standard deviation of 5 kg. Complete for parcels between 65 kg and 80 kg.
questions.hint: Use z = (X − 75)/5 for each value.

questions.q: A normal distribution has a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 5. Complete the table with the percent of data in each interval.
questions.hint: Turn each endpoint into a z-score and add the empirical-rule pieces 34%, 13.5%, 2.35%.

questions.q: The test scores of 28 students are summarised in a frequency table: score 50 (2 students), 60 (6), 70 (12), 80 (6), 90 (2). Can these data be approximated with a normal distribution?
options: No; a normal distribution must have no repeated values
No; the data are skewed to the left
No; the data are skewed to the right
Yes; the data are roughly symmetric and bell-shaped with the highest frequency in the middle
questions.hint: Check where the tallest bar is and whether the two sides mirror each other.
questions.explanation: The highest frequency (12) is at the middle value 70. The frequencies fall off equally on both sides (6, 2 and 6, 2), so the shape is symmetric and bell-shaped. Such data can be approximated by a normal distribution.

questions.q: Each list gives the frequencies of the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in a data set. Match each data set with the best description of its shape.
questions.hint: Look at where the peak is and which way the long tail points.
questions.explanation: 1, 3, 8, 3, 1 peaks in the middle and is symmetric, so it is approximately normal. 15, 8, 4, 2, 1 peaks at the low end with a tail to the right, so it is skewed right. 1, 2, 4, 8, 15 has its tail to the left, so it is skewed left. Equal frequencies give a uniform shape.

questions.q: A survey asked 30 students how many siblings they have. Results: 0 siblings (10 students), 1 (9), 2 (6), 3 (3), 4 (1), 5 (1). Complete the statements.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: The value with the highest frequency is:

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The shape of the distribution is skewed (left or right):

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Can the data be approximated with a normal distribution? (yes/no)

questions.hint: A normal distribution has its peak in the middle and is symmetric.
questions.explanation: The tallest bar is at 0 siblings, and the frequencies keep falling as the values increase, leaving a long tail to the right. So the data are skewed right. A skewed distribution is not symmetric, so it cannot be approximated by a normal distribution.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT represent the point (4, 150°)?
questions.hint: Same point: add multiples of 360° with the same r, or add 180° and change the sign of r.
questions.explanation: 150° − 360° = −210°, so (4, −210°) works. (−4, 330°) and (−4, −30°) point the opposite way from 150° (150° + 180° = 330° ≡ −30°), so they work. (4, −150°) is the same as (4, 210°), a different point.

questions.q: Which of the following DOES represent the point (5, 45°)?
questions.hint: Subtract 360° from the angle, or use −r with the angle plus 180°.
questions.explanation: 45° − 360° = −315°, so (5, −315°) is the same point. (−5, 45°) is the same as (5, 225°), and (−5, 135°) is the same as (5, 315°); neither is (5, 45°).

questions.q: Match each polar point on the left with an equivalent pair on the right.
questions.hint: (−r, θ) is the same point as (r, θ + 180°).

questions.q: Point M has polar coordinates (5, 60°). Which list gives four different polar coordinates for M with −360° ≤ θ ≤ 360°?
questions.hint: With r = −5 you need the opposite direction, 60° + 180° = 240°.
questions.explanation: With r = 5: 60° and 60° − 360° = −300°. With r = −5: 240° and 240° − 360° = −120°. 420° is outside the allowed range, and (−5, 60°) is a different point.

questions.q: Point K has polar coordinates (3, 210°). Write other polar coordinates for K with −360° ≤ θ ≤ 360°.
questions.hint: Subtract 360° to get a negative angle; for −r use the angle 180° away.

questions.q: The point (6, 100°) can also be written as (−6, θ) with −360° ≤ θ < 0°. Find θ in degrees.
questions.hint: The opposite direction to 100° is 280°; then bring it into the range.
questions.explanation: With a negative r the angle must point the opposite way: 100° + 180° = 280°. 280° − 360° = −80°, so the point is (−6, −80°).

questions.q: On a polar grid, points A(3, 45°), B(3, 135°), C(3, 225°), D(3, 315°) and E(3, 90°) are plotted. Match each pair of polar coordinates to the point it names.
questions.hint: (−3, θ) is the same as (3, θ ± 180°).

questions.q: Point P is plotted at (4, 300°). Which other polar coordinates also name P?
questions.hint: A negative r points in the direction 180° away from the angle.
questions.explanation: (−4, 120°) points toward 120° + 180° = 300° with distance 4, so it is P. (−4, 300°) and (4, 120°) are the point (4, 120°), and (−4, −300°) is the point (4, 240°).

questions.q: The point (−5, 75°) is the same as (5, θ) with 0° ≤ θ < 360°. Find θ in degrees.
questions.hint: Add 180° to the angle when you change the sign of r.

questions.q: Find the distance between P₁(4, 20°) and P₂(6, 80°). Round to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Use d = √(r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂cos(θ₂ − θ₁)).

questions.q: Find the distance between P₁(2, 30°) and P₂(5, 150°), to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: The angle between them is 120°, and cos 120° is negative.
questions.explanation: d² = 4 + 25 − 2·2·5·cos 120° = 29 − 20(−0.5) = 39, so d = √39 ≈ 6.2. Using +0.5 for the cosine gives √19 ≈ 4.4 instead.

questions.q: Find the distance between P₁(6, 10°) and P₂(8, 100°).
questions.hint: When the angle difference is 90°, the cosine term is 0.

questions.q: A coast-guard radar shows two ships at (12, 140°) and (5, 80°), where r is in kilometres. Find the distance between the ships to the nearest tenth of a kilometre.
questions.hint: Use the polar distance formula with the angle difference 60°.

questions.q: A radar tracks two drones at (7, 200°) and (4, 110°), with r in kilometres. How far apart are the drones, to the nearest tenth?
questions.hint: The angle difference is 90°, so this is a right-triangle case.
questions.explanation: d² = 49 + 16 − 2·7·4·cos 90° = 65, so d = √65 ≈ 8.1 km. 11.0 and 3.0 come from adding or subtracting the radii.

questions.q: Two boats are at (10, 35°) and (6, 155°) on a radar, with r in kilometres. Find the distance between them.
questions.hint: cos 120° = −1/2, so the cosine term becomes a plus.

questions.q: Two airplanes at the same altitude are at A(9, 20°) and B(12, 50°), with r in kilometres. Regulations say planes must stay at least 7 km apart.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Distance AB to the nearest hundredth (km):

questions.hint: Use d = √(r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂cos(θ₂ − θ₁)) and compare with 7.
questions.explanation: d² = 81 + 144 − 2·9·12·cos 30° = 225 − 216(0.8660) ≈ 37.94. d ≈ 6.16 km, which is less than 7 km, so they are in violation.

questions.q: Two ships are at (6, 100°) and (6, 160°), with r in kilometres. Ships must stay at least 5 km apart. Which statement is correct?
options: No violation: d = 0 km because r is the same
Yes, a violation: d = 12 km is too far
questions.hint: The angle difference is 60°, and both distances are 6.
questions.explanation: d² = 36 + 36 − 2·6·6·cos 60° = 72 − 36 = 36, so d = 6 km. Since 6 km is more than 5 km, there is no violation.

questions.q: Two airplanes are at (15, 0°) and (9, 90°), with r in kilometres. Find the distance between them to the nearest tenth of a kilometre.
questions.hint: With a 90° angle difference, d = √(r₁² + r₂²).

questions.q: For the polar curve r = 4 cos 2θ, complete the table (θ in degrees).
questions.hint: Double the angle, take its cosine, then multiply by 4.
questions.explanation: θ = 30° gives 4 cos 60° = 2; θ = 60° gives 4 cos 120° = −2; θ = 90° gives 4 cos 180° = −4; θ = 135° gives 4 cos 270° = 0; θ = 180° gives 4 cos 360° = 4.

questions.q: For the polar curve r = −6 cos 2θ, what is r when θ = 60°?
questions.hint: Find cos 120° first.

questions.q: For the rose curve r = −2 cos 2θ:
questions.hint: For r = a cos nθ with n even there are 2n petals of length |a|.
questions.explanation: n = 2 is even, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 petals of length |−2| = 2. At θ = 90°, r = −2 cos 180° = 2.

questions.q: For the polar curve r = 4 sin 2θ, complete the table (θ in degrees). Round to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Double the angle, take its sine, then multiply by 4.

questions.q: For the polar curve r = 5 sin 2θ, what is r when θ = 225°?
questions.hint: 2θ = 450°, which is coterminal with 90°.

questions.q: Match each rose curve with its description.
questions.hint: For r = a sin nθ or a cos nθ: n odd gives n petals, n even gives 2n petals, each of length |a|.
questions.explanation: n = 2 gives 4 petals; n = 3 gives 3 petals; n = 4 gives 8 petals; n = 5 gives 5 petals. The petal length is the coefficient |a|.

questions.q: Find the rectangular coordinates of each point with the given polar coordinates.
questions.hint: Use x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, keeping the sign of r.

questions.q: Convert each polar point to rectangular coordinates and plot them: A(3, 0°), B(−2, 90°), C(4, 180°), D(2√2, 135°).
questions.hint: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.

questions.q: Find the rectangular coordinates of the point with polar coordinates (−6, 4π/3). Give exact values as (x, y).
Which of the following are the rectangular coordinates of P(8, π/3)?
questions.hint: x = 8 cos(π/3), y = 8 sin(π/3).
questions.explanation: x = 8 × 1/2 = 4 and y = 8 × √3/2 = 4√3, so P = (4, 4√3). Swapping cos and sin gives (4√3, 4).

questions.q: Find the rectangular coordinates of the point (10, 3π/4). Give exact values as (x, y).
Plot the point with polar coordinates (4√2, 7π/4) on the rectangular grid.
questions.hint: 7π/4 is in Quadrant IV, so x is positive and y is negative.

questions.q: The rectangular form of the polar equation r = 6 sin θ is:
questions.hint: Multiply both sides by r, then use r² = x² + y² and r sin θ = y.
questions.explanation: r² = 6r sin θ gives x² + y² = 6y. Then x² + y² − 6y + 9 = 9, so x² + (y − 3)² = 9.

questions.q: Convert r = −8 cos θ to rectangular form.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Equation in the form (x − h)² + (y − k)² = R²:

questions.hint: Multiply by r and complete the square in x.
questions.explanation: r² = −8r cos θ gives x² + y² = −8x. So x² + 8x + 16 + y² = 16, which is (x + 4)² + y² = 16: centre (−4, 0), radius 4.

questions.q: The polar equation r = 10 sin θ is a circle. Convert it to rectangular form, then plot its centre and its highest and lowest points.
questions.hint: r² = 10r sin θ gives x² + y² = 10y.
questions.explanation: x² + y² = 10y becomes x² + (y − 5)² = 25, a circle with centre (0, 5) and radius 5. The highest point is (0, 10) and the lowest point is (0, 0).

questions.q: Write the rectangular equation (x − 3)² + (y − 4)² = 25 in polar form (r ≠ 0).
questions.hint: Expand, cancel the constants, then substitute x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.
questions.explanation: Expanding: x² − 6x + 9 + y² − 8y + 16 = 25, so x² + y² = 6x + 8y. In polar: r² = 6r cos θ + 8r sin θ, so r = 6 cos θ + 8 sin θ.

questions.q: Write (x + 5)² + (y − 1)² = 26 in polar form r = a cos θ + b sin θ.
questions.hint: After expanding, the constants cancel: 25 + 1 = 26.
questions.explanation: x² + 10x + 25 + y² − 2y + 1 = 26 gives x² + y² = −10x + 2y. So r² = −10r cos θ + 2r sin θ and r = −10 cos θ + 2 sin θ.

questions.q: Write (x − 1)² + (y + 2)² = 5 in the polar form r = a cos θ + b sin θ.
questions.hint: Expand and move the x and y terms to the right side.
questions.explanation: x² − 2x + 1 + y² + 4y + 4 = 5 gives x² + y² = 2x − 4y. So r² = 2r cos θ − 4r sin θ and r = 2 cos θ − 4 sin θ, giving a = 2 and b = −4.

questions.q: Match each polar equation with its rectangular form and graph.
questions.hint: sec θ = 1/cos θ and csc θ = 1/sin θ; for sin θ or cos θ, multiply by r.
questions.explanation: r = 5 sec θ gives r cos θ = 5, so x = 5. r = −4 csc θ gives r sin θ = −4, so y = −4. r² = 6r sin θ gives x² + (y − 3)² = 9. r² = −2r cos θ gives (x + 1)² + y² = 1.

questions.q: Convert r = 3 csc θ to rectangular form and identify the graph.
questions.hint: Multiply both sides by sin θ.
questions.explanation: r = 3/sin θ, so r sin θ = 3, which is y = 3. This is a horizontal line.

questions.q: Convert r = −4 sec θ to rectangular form, then graph it by tapping two points on the line.
questions.hint: Multiply both sides by cos θ.
questions.explanation: r cos θ = −4, so x = −4. This is the vertical line through (−4, 0), for example (−4, 0) and (−4, 2).

questions.q: For z = −1 + √3 i:
questions.hint: |a + bi| = √(a² + b²); check the quadrant before choosing the angle.
questions.explanation: |z| = √(1 + 3) = 2. The point (−1, √3) is in Quadrant II with reference angle 60°, so θ = 180° − 60° = 120°. z = 2(cos 120° + i sin 120°).

questions.q: Express z = 3 − 3i in polar form.
questions.hint: The point (3, −3) is in Quadrant IV.
questions.explanation: r = √(9 + 9) = 3√2. The reference angle is 45°, and in Quadrant IV θ = 360° − 45° = 315°. 18 is r², not r.

questions.q: Graph the complex numbers z₁ = 3 − 4i, z₂ = −2 + 5i and z₃ = −4 − i in the complex plane (horizontal axis real, vertical axis imaginary).
questions.hint: a + bi is plotted at the point (a, b).
questions.explanation: z₁ is at (3, −4), z₂ at (−2, 5) and z₃ at (−4, −1).

questions.q: Find the absolute value |5 − 12i|.
questions.hint: |a + bi| = √(a² + b²).

questions.q: Find the product of z₁ = 4(cos 20° + i sin 20°) and z₂ = 3(cos 40° + i sin 40°). Express in rectangular form a + bi with exact values.
questions.hint: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments.

questions.q: Find z₁z₂ in rectangular form if z₁ = 2√2(cos π/4 + i sin π/4) and z₂ = 3(cos π/2 + i sin π/2).
questions.hint: The product has modulus 6√2 and argument π/4 + π/2.

questions.q: Let z₁ = 5(cos 100° + i sin 100°) and z₂ = 2(cos 50° + i sin 50°). Find z₁z₂.
questions.hint: Multiply the moduli, add the arguments, then use cos 150° and sin 150°.

questions.q: Find z₁ ÷ z₂ in rectangular form if z₁ = 12(cos 150° + i sin 150°) and z₂ = 4(cos 60° + i sin 60°).
questions.hint: Divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.

questions.q: Find z₁ ÷ z₂ in rectangular form if z₁ = 8(cos 300° + i sin 300°) and z₂ = 2(cos 60° + i sin 60°).
questions.hint: Subtract the arguments: 300° − 60°.

questions.q: Let z₁ = 6√2(cos 135° + i sin 135°) and z₂ = 3(cos 45° + i sin 45°). Find z₁ ÷ z₂.
questions.hint: Divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.

questions.q: Find (1 − i)⁴ and write it in rectangular form.
questions.hint: Write 1 − i in polar form, then use De Moivre's theorem.

questions.q: Find (√3 + i)³.
questions.hint: √3 + i has modulus 2 and argument 30°.
questions.explanation: (√3 + i)³ = 2³(cos 90° + i sin 90°) = 8i. Cubing each part separately (3√3 + i) is a common mistake.

questions.q: Use De Moivre's theorem to find (1 + i)⁶.

questions.hint: The number has modulus 1 and argument 45°.
Modulus 1, argument 120°.
questions.explanation: (cos 120° + i sin 120°)⁶ = cos 720° + i sin 720° = cos 0° + i sin 0° = 1.

questions.q: Let z = √2/2 − (√2/2)i = cos(−45°) + i sin(−45°). Complete the table, giving each argument with 0° ≤ θ < 360°.
questions.hint: Multiply −45° by n, then add 360° until the angle is in range.

questions.q: Find (2 + 2√3i)³ and express it in rectangular form.
questions.hint: 2 + 2√3 i has modulus 4 and argument 60°.

questions.q: Find (3 + 3i)⁴ in rectangular form.
Find (−1 + √3i)⁵ using De Moivre's theorem.
questions.hint: −1 + √3 i has modulus 2 and argument 120°.

questions.q: Express −3 + 3i in polar form.
questions.hint: The point (−3, 3) is in Quadrant II.
questions.explanation: r = √(9 + 9) = 3√2. The reference angle is π/4, so in Quadrant II θ = π − π/4 = 3π/4.

questions.q: Express z = −2√3 − 2i in polar form r(cos θ + i sin θ) with 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
questions.hint: Find the reference angle from tan θ = 2/(2√3), then use Quadrant III.
questions.explanation: r = √(12 + 4) = 4. The reference angle is π/6 and the point is in Quadrant III, so θ = π + π/6 = 7π/6.

questions.q: Match each complex number with its polar form.
questions.hint: Find the modulus, then the angle from the quadrant of (a, b).
questions.explanation: 1 + i: r = √2, θ = π/4. −5: r = 5, θ = π. 4i: r = 4, θ = π/2. √3 − i: r = 2, Quadrant IV with reference π/6, so θ = 11π/6.

questions.q: Find the product 4(cos π/6 + i sin π/6) · 3(cos π/3 + i sin π/3).
questions.hint: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments.
questions.explanation: 4 × 3 = 12 and π/6 + π/3 = π/2. So the product is 12(cos π/2 + i sin π/2). Adding the moduli or multiplying the angles are common mistakes.

questions.q: Find the product −5(cos 2π/3 + i sin 2π/3) · 2(cos π/4 + i sin π/4) in the form k(cos θ + i sin θ).
questions.hint: Multiply the numbers in front and add the angles.

questions.q: Find 3(cos 3π/4 + i sin 3π/4) · 2(cos 3π/4 + i sin 3π/4) in rectangular form.
questions.hint: Add the angles: 3π/4 + 3π/4 = 3π/2.
questions.explanation: The product is 6(cos 3π/2 + i sin 3π/2) = 6(0 − i) = −6i.

questions.q: Find the quotient 10(cos 5π/6 + i sin 5π/6) ÷ 2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3).
questions.hint: Divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.
questions.explanation: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 and 5π/6 − π/3 = 5π/6 − 2π/6 = π/2. Adding the angles gives 7π/6, which is the product's angle.

questions.q: Find −8(cos 3π/4 + i sin 3π/4) ÷ 4(cos π/6 + i sin π/6) in the form k(cos θ + i sin θ).
questions.hint: Divide the numbers in front and subtract the angles.

questions.q: Find 9(cos 240° + i sin 240°) ÷ 3(cos 60° + i sin 60°) in rectangular form.
questions.hint: The quotient's angle is 240° − 60°.

questions.q: Find [2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3)]⁶ and express it in rectangular form.
questions.hint: Raise the modulus to the 6th power and multiply the angle by 6.

questions.q: Find [3(cos π/4 + i sin π/4)]² in rectangular form.
questions.hint: Square the modulus and double the angle.
questions.explanation: 3² = 9 and 2 × π/4 = π/2. 9(cos π/2 + i sin π/2) = 9i.

questions.q: Find [2(cos π/6 + i sin π/6)]⁴.
questions.hint: Use De Moivre's theorem: rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).
questions.explanation: 2⁴ = 16 and 4 × π/6 = 2π/3. 16 cos(2π/3) = −8 and 16 sin(2π/3) = 8√3, so the result is −8 + 8√3 i.

questions.q: Find the three cube roots of z = 8. Write each in rectangular form.
questions.hint: 8 = 8(cos 0° + i sin 0°); the cube roots have modulus 2 and are 120° apart.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a cube root of −8?
questions.hint: −8 = 8(cos 180° + i sin 180°), so the roots have angles 60°, 180° and 300°.
questions.explanation: The cube roots are 2(cos 60° + i sin 60°) = 1 + √3 i, 2(cos 180° + i sin 180°) = −2, and 2(cos 300° + i sin 300°) = 1 − √3 i. Since 2³ = 8, not −8, 2 is not a root.

questions.q: Find the four fourth roots of 16 and plot them in the complex plane (real part horizontal, imaginary part vertical). Connect them in order.
questions.hint: The fourth roots have modulus 2 and are 90° apart, starting at 0°.
questions.explanation: 16 = 16(cos 0° + i sin 0°), so the roots are 2(cos 90°k + i sin 90°k) for k = 0, 1, 2, 3: 2, 2i, −2 and −2i. They form a square.

questions.q: Find the first four terms of the sequence aₙ = (−1)ⁿ + 2n.
questions.hint: Substitute n = 1, 2, 3, 4; (−1)ⁿ is −1 for odd n and +1 for even n.

questions.q: Complete the table for the sequence aₙ = (−1)ⁿ · n².
questions.hint: Square n, then make the term negative when n is odd.
questions.explanation: (−1)ⁿ is +1 for even n and −1 for odd n. So a₂ = 4, a₃ = −9, a₄ = 16, a₅ = −25.

questions.q: Plot the first four terms of aₙ = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹ + n as points (n, aₙ).
questions.hint: (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ is +1 when n is odd and −1 when n is even.

questions.q: Find the 6th term of the sequence aₙ = (−1)ⁿ(n + 4).
questions.hint: Substitute n = 6; an even power of −1 is +1.

questions.q: Find the 3rd term of the sequence a₁ = 2, aₙ = (aₙ₋₁)² − 3aₙ₋₁ + 1, n ≥ 2.
questions.hint: Find a₂ first, then use it to find a₃.

questions.q: A sequence is defined by a₁ = 4 and aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ − 5 for n ≥ 2. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Double the previous term, then subtract 5.

questions.q: Find the 3rd term of the sequence a₁ = 1, aₙ = (aₙ₋₁)² − 2aₙ₋₁ − 1, n ≥ 2.
questions.hint: Compute a₂ from a₁, then a₃ from a₂; be careful squaring a negative number.

questions.q: Find the fourth partial sum S₄ of a₁ = 2, aₙ = (aₙ₋₁ − 1)³, n ≥ 2.
questions.hint: Find a₂, a₃ and a₄, then add the first four terms.

questions.q: A sequence is defined by a₁ = 1 and aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 3 for n ≥ 2. Complete the table of terms and partial sums.
questions.hint: Each partial sum is the previous partial sum plus the new term.

questions.q: Find the fourth partial sum of a₁ = −2, aₙ = (aₙ₋₁)² − 5, n ≥ 2.
questions.hint: List a₁ through a₄ before adding.

questions.q: Find the first four terms of the sequence aₙ = 2n² − 3n.
questions.hint: Substitute n = 1, 2, 3, 4 and square before multiplying by 2.

questions.q: Match each sequence formula to its first four terms.
questions.hint: Substitute n = 1, 2, 3, 4 into each formula.
questions.explanation: n² + 1 gives 2, 5, 10, 17. 3n − 1 gives 2, 5, 8, 11. 2ⁿ + 1 gives 3, 5, 9, 17. n³ − 1 gives 0, 7, 26, 63. The list 2, 4, 8, 16 is not used.

questions.q: Find the first four terms of the sequence aₙ = (n + 1)/(n + 2).
questions.hint: Start with n = 1, not n = 0.

questions.q: Plot the first four terms of aₙ = n² − 4n as points (n, aₙ).
questions.hint: Compute a₁ to a₄, then plot each pair (n, aₙ).

questions.q: Find the 4th term of the sequence a₁ = 2, aₙ = −2aₙ₋₁ + 5, n ≥ 2.
questions.hint: Find a₂ and a₃ first.

questions.q: A sequence is defined by a₁ = −3 and aₙ = 4aₙ₋₁ + 6 for n ≥ 2. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Multiply the previous term by 4, then add 6.

questions.q: Find the 4th term of the sequence a₁ = 5, aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ − 8, n ≥ 2.
questions.hint: Apply the rule three times, starting from a₁ = 5.

questions.q: A sequence is defined by a₁ = 3 and aₙ = −aₙ₋₁ + 2 for n ≥ 2. Plot the first four terms as points (n, aₙ).
questions.hint: Change the sign of the previous term, then add 2.

questions.q: Find the fifth partial sum of aₙ = n(n − 2)(n − 5).
questions.hint: Find a₁ to a₅ and add them; watch the signs of the factors.

questions.q: Complete the table of terms and partial sums for aₙ = n² − 6n.
questions.hint: Sₙ = Sₙ₋₁ + aₙ.

questions.q: Find the fifth partial sum of aₙ = 2n(n − 3).
questions.hint: Compute five terms; some of them are negative or zero.

questions.q: Plot the first five terms of the sequence aₙ = 16(−1/2)ⁿ⁻¹ as points (n, aₙ).
questions.hint: Start at 16 and multiply by −1/2 to get each next term.
questions.explanation: The terms are 16, −8, 4, −2, 1. Plot (1, 16), (2, −8), (3, 4), (4, −2), (5, 1). The points alternate above and below the axis and get closer to 0.

questions.q: Match each sequence to its long-run behaviour.
questions.hint: A geometric sequence with |r| < 1 approaches 0; with |r| > 1 it grows without bound.
questions.explanation: 20(1/3)ⁿ⁻¹ has r = 1/3, so it approaches 0. 2(−3)ⁿ has |r| = 3 > 1, so it diverges. 1/n approaches 0, so 3 + 1/n approaches 3. (−0.9)ⁿ has |r| = 0.9 < 1, so it approaches 0.

questions.q: Answer both parts. (i) Is the sequence aₙ = 50(0.8)ⁿ⁻¹ convergent or divergent? (ii) Find the fourth partial sum of aₙ = n² + 2n.
questions.hint: For (i) look at the size of the ratio; for (ii) list four terms and add.
questions.explanation: (i) The ratio 0.8 has |r| < 1, so the terms shrink toward 0 and the sequence is convergent. (ii) The terms are 3, 8, 15, 24, so S₄ = 50.

questions.q: Which statement describes the sequence aₙ = 64(−1/4)ⁿ⁻¹?
questions.hint: Look at the absolute value of the common ratio.
questions.explanation: This is geometric with r = −1/4. Since |r| < 1, the terms alternate in sign but their size shrinks toward 0, so the sequence converges to 0.

questions.q: Answer both parts. (i) Is the sequence aₙ = 3ⁿ/9 convergent or divergent? (ii) Find the fourth partial sum of aₙ = (−2)ⁿ + 3.
questions.hint: For (ii), add the powers of −2 and the four 3s separately.
questions.explanation: (i) 3ⁿ/9 gives 1/3, 1, 3, 9, … which grows without bound, so it is divergent. (ii) (−2) + 4 + (−8) + 16 = 10, and 4 × 3 = 12, so S₄ = 22.

questions.q: Find the fourth partial sum of aₙ = 2(−3)ⁿ⁻¹ + 1.
questions.hint: List the four terms carefully, keeping track of the alternating signs.

questions.q: Plot the first five terms of aₙ = (−2)ⁿ⁻¹ as points (n, aₙ).
questions.hint: Each term is the previous term times −2.
questions.explanation: The terms are 1, −2, 4, −8, 16. The points alternate sides and move further from the axis, which shows the sequence diverges.

questions.q: Which sequence is convergent?
questions.hint: A convergent sequence settles toward one number.
questions.explanation: 5(2/3)ⁿ has ratio 2/3 with |r| < 1, so it approaches 0. (−3)ⁿ/3 and (−1)ⁿ · n grow in size while alternating, and 2n − 7 grows without bound, so those diverge.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the arithmetic sequence 5, 9, 13, 17, …
questions.hint: Use aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d and simplify.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the arithmetic sequence −7, −3, 1, 5, … Simplify to the form aₙ = dn + c.
questions.hint: Find d, then expand a₁ + (n − 1)d.

questions.q: Plot the first five terms of the arithmetic sequence 11, 8, 5, … as points (n, aₙ).
questions.hint: The common difference is −3.
questions.explanation: Subtract 3 each time: 11, 8, 5, 2, −1. Plot (1, 11), (2, 8), (3, 5), (4, 2), (5, −1); the points lie on a straight line.

questions.q: Match each arithmetic sequence to its nth-term formula.
questions.hint: The coefficient of n is the common difference; check n = 1 gives the first term.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series with aₙ = 95, d = 5, n = 18.
questions.hint: First find a₁ from aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series with aₙ = 61, d = 4, n = 15.
questions.hint: Find a₁ first, then use Sₙ = (n/2)(a₁ + aₙ).

questions.q: An arithmetic series has aₙ = −20, d = −3, n = 12. Find a₁ and the sum S₁₂.
questions.hint: a₁ = aₙ − (n − 1)d.

questions.q: Find the 25th term of the arithmetic sequence 7, 11, 15, 19, …
questions.hint: Use aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d with n = 25.

questions.q: Find the 20th term of the arithmetic sequence 40, 33, 26, 19, …
questions.hint: The common difference is negative.

questions.q: For the arithmetic sequence −15, −9, −3, 3, …, complete the table.
questions.hint: aₙ = −15 + 6(n − 1); for the last row solve for n.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the arithmetic sequence with a₅ = 17 and d = 3. Simplify to the form aₙ = dn + c.
questions.hint: Find a₁ from a₅ = a₁ + 4d.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the arithmetic sequence with a₁₀ = −4 and d = −5.
questions.hint: Solve −4 = a₁ + 9(−5) for a₁ first.

questions.q: An arithmetic sequence has a₃ = 1 and d = 2. Plot its first five terms as points (n, aₙ).
questions.hint: Work backwards from a₃ to find a₁.

questions.q: An arithmetic sequence has a₇ = 30 and d = 4. Complete: a₁ = ___ and aₙ = ___ (simplified).
questions.hint: a₇ = a₁ + 6d.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the arithmetic sequence with a₄ = 10 and a₁₂ = 50. Simplify to the form aₙ = dn + c.
questions.hint: The two terms are 12 − 4 = 8 steps apart.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the arithmetic sequence with a₃ = 14 and a₁₀ = −14.
questions.hint: Find d from the 7 steps between a₃ and a₁₀.

questions.q: An arithmetic sequence has a₅ = −3 and a₁₅ = 47. Find d, a₁ and the nth-term equation.
questions.hint: a₁₅ − a₅ = 10d.

questions.q: Find four arithmetic means between 7 and 42.
questions.hint: With four means there are 6 terms in total, so 42 = 7 + 5d.
questions.explanation: 42 = 7 + 5d gives d = 7. The means are 14, 21, 28, 35.

questions.q: Insert three arithmetic means between 50 and 2. Complete the table.
questions.hint: There are 5 terms, so 2 = 50 + 4d.
questions.explanation: 2 = 50 + 4d gives d = −12. The means are 38, 26, 14.

questions.q: Find three arithmetic means between −9 and 15.
questions.hint: Three means make 5 terms in total.
questions.explanation: 15 = −9 + 4d, so d = 6. The means are −3, 3, 9.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series 5 + 9 + 13 + … + 81.
questions.hint: Find how many terms there are first.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series −30 + (−26) + (−22) + … + 50.
questions.hint: Solve 50 = −30 + (n − 1)(4) for n.

questions.q: For the arithmetic series 40 + 35 + 30 + … + (−25), find the number of terms and the sum.
questions.hint: The common difference is −5.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series with a₁ = −10, d = 4, n = 20.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = (n/2)(2a₁ + (n − 1)d).

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series with a₁ = 50, d = −3, n = 30.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = (n/2)(2a₁ + (n − 1)d) and be careful with the negative d.

questions.q: An arithmetic series has a₁ = 3 and d = 5. Complete the table of partial sums.
An arithmetic series has a₁ = 12, aₙ = 96 and Sₙ = 810. Find n, d and the next two terms after a₁.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = (n/2)(a₁ + aₙ) to find n, then aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d.
questions.explanation: 810 = (n/2)(108), so n = 15. 96 = 12 + 14d, so d = 6. The first three terms are 12, 18, 24.

questions.q: Find the first three terms of the arithmetic series with a₁ = 5, aₙ = 77, Sₙ = 533.
questions.hint: Find n from the sum formula before finding d.
questions.explanation: 533 = (n/2)(5 + 77) = 41n, so n = 13. 77 = 5 + 12d, so d = 6. The first three terms are 5, 11, 17.

questions.q: Each row describes an arithmetic series. Complete the table.
questions.hint: n = 2Sₙ/(a₁ + aₙ), then d = (aₙ − a₁)/(n − 1).

questions.q: An arithmetic series has aₙ = 85, n = 15 and Sₙ = 750. Find a₁, d and the next two terms.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = (n/2)(a₁ + aₙ) to find a₁.
questions.explanation: 750 = 7.5(a₁ + 85), so a₁ + 85 = 100 and a₁ = 15. 85 = 15 + 14d, so d = 5. The first three terms are 15, 20, 25.

questions.q: Find the first three terms of the arithmetic series with aₙ = −40, n = 11, Sₙ = −165.
questions.hint: Find a₁ from the sum, then d from the last term.
questions.explanation: −165 = 5.5(a₁ − 40), so a₁ − 40 = −30 and a₁ = 10. −40 = 10 + 10d, so d = −5. The first three terms are 10, 5, 0.

questions.q: An arithmetic series has aₙ = 100, n = 25 and Sₙ = 1600. Find the third term a₃.
questions.hint: Find a₁ and d first.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series Σ (3k + 2) from k = 1 to 20.
questions.hint: Find the first and last terms, then use Sₙ = (n/2)(first + last).
questions.explanation: There are 20 terms. First term 3(1) + 2 = 5, last term 3(20) + 2 = 62. Sum = 10(5 + 62) = 670.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series Σ (5 − 2k) from k = 1 to 12.
questions.hint: The first term is at k = 1 and the last at k = 12.

questions.q: Complete the table for each arithmetic series.
questions.hint: Substitute the lower and upper limits for the first and last terms.
questions.explanation: Series 1: first 9, last 27, sum = 5(9 + 27) = 180. Series 2: first 2, last 86, sum = 7.5(2 + 86) = 660.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series Σ (3k − 1) from k = 5 to 14.
questions.hint: The number of terms is 14 − 5 + 1.
questions.explanation: There are 10 terms. First term 3(5) − 1 = 14, last term 3(14) − 1 = 41. Sum = 5(14 + 41) = 275.

questions.q: Find the sum of the arithmetic series Σ (2k + 5) from k = 3 to 10.
questions.hint: Count the terms carefully: from k = 3 to k = 10.
questions.explanation: There are 10 − 3 + 1 = 8 terms. First term 11, last term 25. Sum = 4(11 + 25) = 144.

questions.q: For the series Σ (4k + 3) from k = 6 to 20, find the number of terms, the first term, the last term and the sum.
questions.hint: Number of terms = upper − lower + 1.

questions.q: Mariam saves AED 200 in the first month and increases her savings by AED 25 each month. How much does she save in total over 12 months? Give the amount in AED.
questions.hint: Find the 12th month's amount, then use Sₙ = (n/2)(a₁ + aₙ).

questions.q: A theatre has 18 seats in the first row, and each row has 3 more seats than the row before. How many seats are there in 20 rows?
questions.hint: Find the number of seats in row 20 first.

questions.q: A weekly quiz prize starts at AED 300 and rises by AED 40 each week. Complete the table (amounts in AED).
questions.hint: Prize in week n is 300 + 40(n − 1); the total is (n/2)(first + that week's prize).

questions.q: A ball rolling down a long ramp travels 5 m in the first second, 15 m in the next second and 25 m in the third second. If the pattern continues, how many metres does it travel in total in 8 seconds?
questions.hint: The distances per second form an arithmetic sequence with d = 10.

questions.q: An object in free fall travels 4.9 m in the 1st second, 14.7 m in the 2nd second and 24.5 m in the 3rd second. How far does it travel during the 12th second alone?
questions.hint: Find the 12th term of the arithmetic sequence, not the sum.

questions.q: A cart travels 5 m in the 1st second, 15 m in the 2nd second, 25 m in the 3rd second, and so on. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Distance in second n is 5 + 10(n − 1); total is (n/2)(5 + that distance).
questions.explanation: Second 2 total: 5 + 15 = 20. Second 4: 5 + 30 = 35 m, total 2(5 + 35) = 80 m. Second 6: 5 + 50 = 55 m, total 3(5 + 55) = 180 m.

questions.q: Find a₁ for the geometric series with Sₙ = 2186, aₙ = 1458, r = 3.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = (r·aₙ − a₁)/(r − 1).

questions.q: Find a₁ for the geometric series with Sₙ = 381, aₙ = 192, r = 2.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = (r·aₙ − a₁)/(r − 1).

questions.q: A geometric series has Sₙ = 121, aₙ = 1 and r = 1/3. Find a₁ and the number of terms n.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = (a₁ − r·aₙ)/(1 − r), then find n from aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹.

questions.q: Find aₙ for the geometric sequence a₁ = 1215, r = 1/3, n = 5.
questions.hint: aₙ = a₁ · rⁿ⁻¹.

questions.q: Find aₙ for the geometric sequence a₁ = −2, r = 3, n = 6.
questions.hint: The exponent is n − 1 = 5.

questions.q: A geometric sequence has a₁ = 5 and r = −2. Complete the table.
questions.hint: aₙ = 5(−2)ⁿ⁻¹; an odd exponent keeps the negative sign.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the geometric sequence 4, −12, 36, …
questions.hint: Find r by dividing a term by the one before it.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the geometric sequence 200, 100, 50, … in the form aₙ = a₁ · rⁿ⁻¹.
questions.hint: Divide the second term by the first to get r.

questions.q: Match each geometric sequence to its nth-term formula.
questions.hint: The coefficient is the first term and the base is the common ratio.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the geometric sequence with a₄ = 54 and r = 3.
questions.hint: a₄ = a₁ · r³.
questions.explanation: 54 = a₁ × 3³ = 27a₁, so a₁ = 2. aₙ = 2(3)ⁿ⁻¹.

questions.q: Write the equation of the nth term of the geometric sequence with a₅ = 48 and r = −2.
questions.hint: a₅ = a₁(−2)⁴, and (−2)⁴ is positive.

questions.q: A geometric sequence has a₃ = 12 and r = 1/2. Find a₁ and a₆.
questions.hint: a₃ = a₁ · r².

questions.q: Find three positive geometric means between 3 and 768.
questions.hint: With three means there are 5 terms, so 768 = 3r⁴.
questions.explanation: r⁴ = 768/3 = 256, so r = 4. The means are 12, 48, 192.

questions.q: Find two geometric means between 5 and 135.
questions.hint: Two means make 4 terms, so 135 = 5r³.
questions.explanation: r³ = 135/5 = 27, so r = 3. The means are 5 × 3 = 15 and 15 × 3 = 45.

questions.q: Fill in the missing geometric means (use the positive common ratio).
questions.hint: a₅ = a₁r⁴; solve for r first.

questions.q: Find the sum of the geometric series with a₁ = 3, r = 2, n = 8.
Find the sum of the geometric series with a₁ = 81, r = 1/3, n = 5.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) and remember to divide by 1 − r = 2/3.

questions.q: A geometric series has a₁ = 1 and r = −2. Complete the table of partial sums.
Find the sum of the geometric series Σ 2(3)ᵏ⁻¹ from k = 1 to 6.
questions.hint: Identify a₁, r and n, then use Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).

questions.q: Find the sum of the geometric series Σ 5(−2)ᵏ⁻¹ from k = 1 to 5.
For the series Σ 64(1/2)ᵏ⁻¹ from k = 1 to 4, identify a₁, r and find the sum.
questions.hint: Substitute k = 1 for the first term; the base of the power is r.
questions.explanation: a₁ = 64 and r = 1/2. The terms are 64, 32, 16, 8, so the sum is 120.

questions.q: Find a₁ for the geometric series with Sₙ = 1092, r = 3, n = 6.
questions.hint: Substitute into Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) and solve for a₁.

questions.q: Find a₁ for the geometric series with Sₙ = −1023, r = 2, n = 10.
A geometric series has Sₙ = 340, r = 4, n = 4. Find a₁ and a₄.
questions.hint: Compute (1 − 4⁴)/(1 − 4) first.

questions.q: Fatima saves 5 AED in the first week. Each week after that she saves three times as much as the week before. How much has she saved in total after 4 weeks? Give the amount in AED.
questions.hint: Add the first 4 terms of a geometric sequence with a = 5 and r = 3.
questions.explanation: The weekly amounts are 5, 15, 45, 135. Using S₄ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) = 5(3⁴ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 5(80)/2 = 200. She has saved 200 AED.

questions.q: A lake's water level rises 4 cm on day 1, and each day after that it rises twice as much as the day before. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Each day's rise is double the previous day; the total is the running sum.
questions.explanation: The daily rises form a geometric sequence 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 (r = 2). Running totals: 4, 12, 28, 60, 124. Check: S₅ = 4(2⁵ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 4 × 31 = 124 cm.

questions.q: A plant grows 2 cm in its first week. Each week after that it grows three times as much as it did the week before. What is its total growth after 5 weeks?
questions.hint: Use S₅ = a(r⁵ − 1)/(r − 1) with a = 2 and r = 3.
questions.explanation: The weekly growths are 2, 6, 18, 54, 162. S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 2(242)/2 = 242 cm. 162 cm is only the growth in week 5, and 728 cm would be the total after 6 weeks.

questions.q: A river rises 1 cm on day 1, and each day after that it rises twice as much as the day before. Plot the points (n, rise on day n) for days n = 1, 2, 3 and 4.
questions.hint: The rise on day n is 1 × 2^(n − 1).
questions.explanation: The daily rises are 1, 2, 4, 8 cm, so the points are (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 4) and (4, 8). The points curve upward because each term is double the previous one.

questions.q: The first swing of a pendulum travels 40 cm. Each swing after that travels 90% as far as the swing before. Find the total distance traveled in the first 10 swings. Round to the nearest tenth of a centimeter.
questions.hint: Use Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) with a = 40, r = 0.9 and n = 10.
questions.explanation: S₁₀ = 40(1 − 0.9¹⁰)/(1 − 0.9). Since 0.9¹⁰ ≈ 0.348678, S₁₀ ≈ 40(0.651322)/0.1 ≈ 260.53. Rounded, the pendulum travels about 260.5 cm.

questions.q: A ball rolls 50 m in the first minute and each minute it rolls 80% as far as in the previous minute. How far has it rolled after 8 minutes? (Nearest tenth.)
questions.hint: Add 8 terms of a geometric sequence with a = 50 and r = 0.8.
questions.explanation: S₈ = 50(1 − 0.8⁸)/(1 − 0.8) = 250(1 − 0.16777216) ≈ 208.06, so about 208.1 m. 250 m is the sum of infinitely many terms, and 10.5 m is just the 8th term.

questions.q: The finite series 20 + 15 + 11.25 + … has 6 terms. Complete each blank.
questions.hint: Divide the second term by the first to get r, then use Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r).

questions.q: A swing travels 64 cm on its first pass, and each pass travels 3/4 as far as the one before. Complete the table.

questions.q: Find the sum of each infinite series if it exists. Type 'does not exist' if there is no sum. (a) 20 + 16 + 12.8 + …   (b) 5 + 7.5 + 11.25 + …
questions.hint: Find r for each series; a sum exists only when |r| < 1.
questions.explanation: (a) r = 16/20 = 0.8, so S = 20/(1 − 0.8) = 20/0.2 = 100. (b) r = 7.5/5 = 1.5 and |1.5| ≥ 1, so the series diverges and has no sum.

questions.q: Find the sum of the infinite series 9/4 + 3/4 + 1/4 + …
questions.hint: The common ratio is (3/4) ÷ (9/4).
questions.explanation: r = (3/4)/(9/4) = 1/3, and |1/3| < 1 so the sum exists. S = (9/4)/(1 − 1/3) = (9/4)/(2/3) = 27/8. 13/4 is only the sum of the first three terms.

questions.q: Complete the table for each infinite geometric series. Write the sum as a fraction or decimal, or 'does not exist'.

questions.q: Find each sum if it exists (type 'does not exist' if it does not). (a) Σ from k = 1 to ∞ of 5(2/3)^(k−1)   (b) Σ from k = 1 to ∞ of (1/2)(7/4)^(k−1)
questions.hint: Read a as the value when k = 1 and r as the base of the power.

questions.q: Find Σ from k = 1 to ∞ of 6(−1/2)^(k−1).
questions.hint: Here r is negative; keep the sign when you compute 1 − r.

questions.q: A puck slides 90 m in the first minute after being hit. Each minute it slides only 1/3 as far as in the minute before. What total distance does it slide? Give your answer in meters.
questions.hint: This is an infinite geometric series with a = 90 and r = 1/3.
questions.explanation: S = a/(1 − r) = 90/(1 − 1/3) = 90/(2/3) = 135. The puck slides 135 m in total.

questions.q: A toy car rolls 50 m in the first minute. Each minute after that it rolls 80% as far as in the previous minute. How far does it roll in total?
questions.hint: Use S = a/(1 − r) with r = 0.8.
questions.explanation: S = 50/(1 − 0.8) = 50/0.2 = 250 m. 62.5 m comes from dividing by 0.8 instead of 0.2, and 90 m is only the first two minutes. Since |r| < 1 the total is finite.

questions.q: A ball travels 200 m in minute 1, and each minute it travels half as far as the minute before. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Halve each distance; the infinite total is a/(1 − r).
questions.explanation: Distances: 200, 100, 50, 25. Totals: 200, 300, 350, 375. The total over all minutes is 200/(1 − 1/2) = 400 m.

questions.q: A pendulum travels 20 cm on its first swing and 90% of the previous distance on each swing after that. Find the total distance it travels before coming to rest, in centimeters.

questions.q: A pendulum travels 15 cm on its first swing and each swing after that is 96% of the one before. What total distance does it travel before it stops?
questions.explanation: S = 15/(1 − 0.96) = 15/0.04 = 375 cm. 15.625 cm comes from 15 ÷ 0.96, and 360 cm uses the second swing (14.4 cm) as the first term.

questions.hint: Add 8, 4, 2, 1 one at a time.
questions.explanation: S₁ = 8, S₂ = 12, S₃ = 14, S₄ = 15. The points approach the line y = 16, which is the infinite sum 8/(1 − 1/2) = 16.

questions.q: A rechargeable battery lasts 10 hours on its first charge, and each recharge restores 99.5% of the previous capacity. How many total hours should the battery last over its lifetime?

questions.q: A phone battery gives 12 hours on its first charge, and each recharge gives 99.8% of the previous capacity. What total number of hours should it last?
questions.explanation: S = 12/(1 − 0.998) = 12/0.002 = 6000 hours. The other choices come from misplacing the decimal (0.02 or 0.0002) or dividing by 0.998.

questions.q: Each row describes a battery whose capacity after each recharge is the given percent of the previous capacity. Complete the table (total = sum of all charges).
questions.hint: Total = first charge ÷ (1 − r); to find the first charge, multiply the total by (1 − r).

questions.q: f(x) = x + 3 for x < 1, f(1) = 2, and f(x) = x² for x > 1. Which statements are true? I. lim (x→1⁻) f(x) = 4   II. lim (x→1) f(x) = 2   III. lim (x→1⁺) f(x) = 1
questions.hint: Find each one-sided limit separately; f(1) does not decide the limit.
questions.explanation: From the left, x + 3 → 4, so I is true. From the right, x² → 1, so III is true. The one-sided limits differ (4 ≠ 1), so lim (x→1) f(x) does not exist and II is false.

questions.q: h(x) = x² for x < −1, h(−1) = 3, and h(x) = x + 2 for x > −1. Match each quantity to its value.
questions.hint: Use the piece that applies on the side you approach from.
questions.explanation: From the left of −1, x² → 1. h(−1) is defined as 3. Near x = 2 we use x + 2 → 4. Near x = −3 we use x² → 9.

questions.q: The graph of p is made of two line segments: for −4 ≤ x ≤ 0 it is y = x + 3 (with a filled dot at (0, 3)), and for 0 < x ≤ 4 it is y = x − 2 (with an open circle at (0, −2)). Type 'DNE' if a limit does not exist.
questions.hint: Compare the y-values the graph approaches from each side.
questions.explanation: From the left, x + 3 → 3; from the right, x − 2 → −2. Since 3 ≠ −2 the two-sided limit at 0 does not exist. Near x = 2 the graph is y = x − 2, so the limit is 0.

questions.q: f(x) = −x² + 4 for x < 2, f(2) = 3, and f(x) = x − 5 for x > 2. Find each value.
questions.hint: Use x − 5 from the right and −x² + 4 from the left.
questions.explanation: From the right, 2 − 5 = −3. From the left, −(2)² + 4 = 0. The value f(2) = 3 is given directly and does not affect the limits.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x for x < 1 and f(x) = x + 3 for x ≥ 1. Complete the table, then give the one-sided limits at x = 1.
questions.hint: Values below 1 use 2x; values above 1 use x + 3.
questions.explanation: 2(0.9) = 1.8 and 2(0.99) = 1.98, approaching 2 from the left. 1.01 + 3 = 4.01 and 1.1 + 3 = 4.1, approaching 4 from the right. So the left limit is 2 and the right limit is 4.

questions.q: On the graph of g, the curve coming from the left ends in an open circle at (3, −1). The curve to the right starts with an open circle at (3, 2). There is a filled dot at (3, 4). Find lim (x→3⁺) g(x).
questions.hint: A right-hand limit only looks at the part of the graph with x > 3.
questions.explanation: Approaching x = 3 from the right, the graph heads toward the open circle at (3, 2), so the limit is 2. −1 is the left-hand limit and 4 is g(3).

questions.q: A curve has an open circle at (−2, 5), and the curve passes smoothly into that circle from both sides. There is no filled dot at x = −2. Find lim (x→−2⁻) f(x).
questions.hint: A limit depends on the y-value the graph approaches, not on whether the point is filled.
questions.explanation: From the left, the curve approaches the open circle at height 5, so the left-hand limit is 5 even though f(−2) is undefined.

questions.q: k(x) = x² + 1 for x ≠ 3, and k(3) = 0. Find lim (x→3⁻) k(x).
questions.hint: Near x = 3 (but not at 3) k(x) = x² + 1.
questions.explanation: As x → 3 from the left, x² + 1 → 9 + 1 = 10. The value k(3) = 0 does not change the limit, so the answer is 10.

questions.q: The graph of f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is the line y = x + 2 with one hole. Plot the location of the hole; its y-coordinate equals lim (x→2) f(x).
questions.hint: Simplify f(x) for x ≠ 2, then substitute x = 2.
questions.explanation: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2. The hole is at x = 2, where x + 2 = 4, so plot (2, 4). Both one-sided limits at 2 equal 4.

questions.q: A continuous-looking curve has an open circle at (1, 3) and a separate filled dot at (1, −1). Find lim (x→1) f(x).
questions.hint: Both sides of the curve approach the same height.
questions.explanation: From both sides the curve approaches the open circle at height 3, so lim (x→1) f(x) = 3. The filled dot only tells us f(1) = −1.

questions.q: The graph of f is the line y = x + 3 except for an open circle at (2, 5), and there is a filled dot at (2, 1). Find lim (x→2) f(x).
questions.hint: Follow the line toward x = 2 from both sides.
questions.explanation: Both sides of the line approach y = 2 + 3 = 5, so the limit is 5. f(2) = 1 is a different value and does not affect the limit.

questions.q: Match each description of a graph near x = a to lim (x→a) f(x).

left: left side → −3, right side → −3, f(a) undefined

questions.hint: The two-sided limit exists only when both sides approach the same value.
questions.explanation: Rows 1, 3 and 4 have equal one-sided limits, so the limit is that common value: 4, −3 and 0. In row 2 the sides approach 2 and 6, so the limit does not exist. The value f(a) never decides the limit.

questions.q: h(x) = 2x − 7 for x < 6, h(6) = 2, and h(x) = 17 − 2x for x > 6. Find lim (x→6⁻) h(x).
questions.hint: From the left use 2x − 7.
questions.explanation: As x → 6 from the left, 2(6) − 7 = 5. So the left-hand limit is 5, even though h(6) = 2.

questions.q: On a graph, the curve coming from the left ends in an open circle at (4, −3). A new piece starts at a filled dot at (4, 1) and continues to the right. Find lim (x→4⁻) f(x).
questions.hint: Look only at the piece to the left of x = 4.
questions.explanation: The left piece approaches height −3, so the left-hand limit is −3. The right-hand limit and f(4) are both 1, and the two-sided limit does not exist, but that was not asked.

questions.q: f(x) = x² − 3 for x < 3 and f(x) = 2x for x ≥ 3. Find each value. Type 'DNE' if a limit does not exist.
questions.hint: Substitute x = 3 into each piece.
questions.explanation: Left: 3² − 3 = 6. Right: 2(3) = 6. The one-sided limits agree, so the limit is 6, and f(3) = 2(3) = 6 as well.

questions.q: q(x) = x² − 4 for x ≠ 6, and q(6) = 2. Find lim (x→6) q(x).
questions.hint: The limit uses the values of q near 6, not at 6.
questions.explanation: Near x = 6, q(x) = x² − 4 → 36 − 4 = 32 from both sides, so the limit is 32. q(6) = 2 is irrelevant to the limit.

questions.q: On a graph, the curve approaches an open circle at (−1, 4) from both the left and the right, and there is a filled dot at (−1, 0). Find lim (x→−1) f(x). Type 'DNE' if it does not exist.
questions.hint: Do both sides approach the same height?
questions.explanation: Both sides approach height 4, so lim (x→−1) f(x) = 4. The filled dot shows f(−1) = 0, which does not affect the limit.

questions.q: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 6, f(6) = 5, and f(x) = 13 − x for x > 6. Complete the table (type 'DNE' if a limit does not exist).
questions.hint: Find each one-sided limit first.
questions.explanation: Left: 6 + 1 = 7. Right: 13 − 6 = 7. Both sides agree, so the limit is 7. The function value is f(6) = 5, so f is not continuous at 6.

questions.q: On a graph there is an open circle at (−2, 3) on the curve and a filled dot at (−2, −1). Find f(−2).
questions.hint: A function value is shown by the filled dot.
questions.explanation: The filled dot tells us the actual value: f(−2) = −1. The open circle at height 3 is where the curve approaches, which is the limit, not the value.

questions.q: g(x) = 3 − x for x < 1, g(1) = 5, and g(x) = x + 1 for x > 1. Complete each blank.
questions.hint: g(1) is given by its own line; the limit uses the pieces on each side.
questions.explanation: g(1) = 5 is defined directly. From the left 3 − 1 = 2 and from the right 1 + 1 = 2, so the limit is 2. g(0) uses the first piece: 3 − 0 = 3.

questions.q: Match each graph description to the value of f(4).

left: open circle at (4, 2) and filled dot at (4, −3)
open circle at (4, 6) and no other point with x = 4

questions.hint: Only a filled point (or a point on an unbroken curve) gives the value of f.
questions.explanation: In the first case the filled dot gives f(4) = −3. In the second, the point (4, 1) is on the curve, so f(4) = 1. In the third there is no point on the graph at x = 4, so f(4) is undefined.

questions.q: Evaluate lim (x→3) |x − 3|/(x − 3).
questions.hint: Compare the values for x slightly above 3 and slightly below 3.
questions.explanation: For x > 3, |x − 3| = x − 3, so the quotient is 1. For x < 3, |x − 3| = −(x − 3), so the quotient is −1. The one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist.

questions.q: For f(x) = |x|/x, find each limit. Type 'DNE' if it does not exist.
questions.hint: Replace |x| by x or by −x depending on the side.
questions.explanation: For x > 0, |x|/x = x/x = 1. For x < 0, |x|/x = −x/x = −1. Since 1 ≠ −1, the two-sided limit does not exist.

questions.q: Complete the table for f(x) = |x − 2|/(x − 2). Type 'DNE' if a limit does not exist.
questions.hint: The numerator is always positive; the denominator's sign depends on the side.
questions.explanation: For x < 2, x − 2 is negative, so f(x) = −1. For x > 2, f(x) = 1. The left and right values are −1 and 1, so lim (x→2) f(x) does not exist.

questions.q: Find lim (x→−5⁻) |x + 5| / (2(x + 5)). Give an exact value.
questions.hint: For x < −5, x + 5 is negative.
questions.explanation: For x < −5, |x + 5| = −(x + 5), so the expression is −(x + 5)/(2(x + 5)) = −1/2. The left-hand limit is −1/2.

questions.q: Use the Sandwich theorem to evaluate lim (x→0) [x² cos(1/x) + 5].
questions.hint: Use −1 ≤ cos(1/x) ≤ 1.
questions.explanation: Since −1 ≤ cos(1/x) ≤ 1, we get −x² ≤ x² cos(1/x) ≤ x², so 5 − x² ≤ x² cos(1/x) + 5 ≤ 5 + x². Both bounds approach 5 as x → 0, so the limit is 5.

questions.q: Evaluate lim (x→0) [x⁴ sin(3/x) − 2].
questions.hint: Bound sin(3/x) between −1 and 1.
questions.explanation: −x⁴ ≤ x⁴ sin(3/x) ≤ x⁴ and both bounds go to 0, so x⁴ sin(3/x) → 0 by the Sandwich theorem. The limit is 0 − 2 = −2.

questions.q: Use the Sandwich theorem on g(x) = x² sin(1/x) + 7 as x → 0. Complete each blank.
questions.hint: Start from −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1, multiply by x², then add 7.
questions.explanation: −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x², so 7 − x² ≤ g(x) ≤ 7 + x². Both bounds approach 7 as x → 0, so the limit of g is 7.

questions.q: Match each limit as x → 0 to its value.
questions.hint: A bounded factor times something that goes to 0 goes to 0.
questions.explanation: x sin(1/x) is squeezed between −|x| and |x|, so it → 0. The x² terms in the next two also → 0, giving 3 and −4. sin(1/x) itself keeps oscillating between −1 and 1, so its limit does not exist.

questions.q: f(x) = 3x − 1 for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = x² + 1 for x > 2. Find lim (x→2) f(x). Type 'DNE' if it does not exist.
questions.hint: Find both one-sided limits at x = 2.
questions.explanation: Left: 3(2) − 1 = 5. Right: 2² + 1 = 5. Both sides agree, so lim (x→2) f(x) = 5.

questions.q: g(x) = x² for x < −2 and g(x) = 3x + 1 for x ≥ −2. Find lim (x→−2) g(x).
questions.hint: Compare (−2)² with 3(−2) + 1.
questions.explanation: Left: (−2)² = 4. Right: 3(−2) + 1 = −5. Since 4 ≠ −5, the limit does not exist.

questions.q: For each piecewise function, find the one-sided limits at the given point and the two-sided limit. Type 'DNE' if a limit does not exist.

questions.hint: Substitute the point into the piece used on each side.
questions.explanation: Row 1: 2(1) + 3 = 5 and 6 − 1 = 5, so the limit is 5. Row 2: 3² = 9 and 3 + 5 = 8 differ, so the limit does not exist. Row 3: 4 − 0 = 4 and 4 + 0 = 4, so the limit is 4.

questions.explanation: Right: 2² − 1 = 3. Left: 2k + 1. Setting 2k + 1 = 3 gives k = 1.

questions.q: f(x) = x² − 10 for x ≤ 4 and f(x) = 24/x for x > 4. Find lim (x→4) f(x).
questions.hint: Evaluate each piece at x = 4.
questions.explanation: Left: 4² − 10 = 6. Right: 24/4 = 6. Both one-sided limits are 6, so the limit is 6.

questions.q: f(x) = 1 − x² for x ≤ −2 and f(x) = 6/x for x > −2. Find lim (x→−2) f(x). Type 'DNE' if it does not exist.
questions.hint: Evaluate each piece at x = −2.
questions.explanation: Left: 1 − (−2)² = 1 − 4 = −3. Right: 6/(−2) = −3. The one-sided limits agree, so the limit is −3.

questions.q: Match each piecewise function to lim f(x) at the point where the formula changes.

left: x² if x ≤ 2; 8/x if x > 2 (at x = 2)
2x if x < 3; x + 4 if x ≥ 3 (at x = 3)

questions.hint: The limit exists only if both pieces give the same value at the point.
questions.explanation: At 1: 1 + 4 = 5 and 10/2 = 5, so the limit is 5. At 2: 2² = 4 and 8/2 = 4, so the limit is 4. At 3: 2(3) = 6 but 3 + 4 = 7, so the limit does not exist.

questions.q: Find lim (x→0) tan(2x)/(5x).
questions.hint: Rewrite as (2/5) · tan(2x)/(2x).
questions.explanation: tan(2x)/(5x) = (2/5) · [tan(2x)/(2x)], and tan(u)/u → 1 as u → 0. So the limit is 2/5.

questions.q: Find lim (x→0) sin(4x)/x.
questions.hint: Multiply and divide by 4.
questions.explanation: sin(4x)/x = 4 · [sin(4x)/(4x)], and sin(u)/u → 1 as u → 0. So the limit is 4 × 1 = 4.

questions.q: Match each limit as x → 0 to its value.
questions.hint: Use sin(u)/u → 1 and tan(u)/u → 1 as u → 0.

questions.q: Find lim (x→0) [2 − x sin(1/x)].
questions.hint: Show x sin(1/x) → 0 first.
questions.explanation: −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x|, and both bounds go to 0, so x sin(1/x) → 0 by the Sandwich theorem. The limit is 2 − 0 = 2.

questions.q: Find lim (x→0) [x³ sin(1/x²) − 6].
questions.hint: Bound sin(1/x²) between −1 and 1, then multiply by |x³|.
questions.explanation: −|x³| ≤ x³ sin(1/x²) ≤ |x³|, and both bounds go to 0, so that term → 0. The limit is 0 − 6 = −6.

questions.explanation: e^(3x) − 1 = (e^x − 1)(e^(2x) + e^x + 1). Cancelling e^x − 1 leaves e^(2x) + e^x + 1, which → 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 as x → 0.

questions.explanation: e^(2x) − 1 = (e^x − 1)(e^x + 1). After cancelling, the expression is e^x + 1, which → 1 + 1 = 2.

questions.q: If lim (x→a) f(x) = 2 and lim (x→a) g(x) = −3, find lim (x→a) ([f(x)]² + g(x))/(g(x) − 1).
questions.hint: Substitute the limits into the expression using the limit laws.
questions.explanation: Numerator: 2² + (−3) = 1. Denominator: −3 − 1 = −4. The limit is 1/(−4) = −1/4. The choice −7/4 comes from using +3 instead of −3 in the numerator.

questions.q: If lim (x→a) f(x) = −2 and lim (x→a) g(x) = 5, find lim (x→a) [3f(x) − g(x)] · g(x).
questions.hint: Find the limit of each factor, then multiply.
questions.explanation: 3f − g → 3(−2) − 5 = −11, and g → 5. By the product law, the limit is (−11)(5) = −55.

questions.q: Given lim (x→a) f(x) = 4 and lim (x→a) g(x) = −2, complete the table of limits as x → a.
questions.hint: Apply the sum, product, quotient, root and power laws.

questions.q: Compute lim (x→16) (x − 16)/(√x − 4).
questions.hint: Factor x − 16 as (√x − 4)(√x + 4).
questions.explanation: (x − 16)/(√x − 4) = √x + 4 for x ≠ 16. Substituting x = 16 gives 4 + 4 = 8.

questions.q: Compute lim (x→4) (√x − 2)/(x − 4). Give an exact value.
questions.explanation: (√x − 2)/(x − 4) = 1/(√x + 2) for x ≠ 4. Substituting gives 1/(2 + 2) = 1/4.

questions.q: Evaluate lim (x→0) (√(x + 9) − 3)/x by rationalizing.
questions.hint: Use the conjugate of the numerator.
questions.explanation: Multiplying by √(x + 9) + 3 gives (x + 9 − 9)/(x(√(x + 9) + 3)) = 1/(√(x + 9) + 3). Substituting x = 0 gives 1/(3 + 3) = 1/6.

questions.q: Match each limit to its value.
questions.hint: Factor or multiply by the conjugate, then substitute.

questions.q: Evaluate lim (x→−2) (x² + 5x + 6)/(x + 2).
questions.hint: Factor the numerator.
questions.explanation: x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3), so the expression equals x + 3 for x ≠ −2. Substituting gives −2 + 3 = 1.

questions.q: Evaluate lim (x→4) (x² − 16)/(x − 4).
questions.hint: Use the difference of squares.
questions.explanation: (x² − 16)/(x − 4) = (x − 4)(x + 4)/(x − 4) = x + 4 for x ≠ 4. Substituting gives 8.

questions.q: Complete the table for f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) and use it to estimate lim (x→1) f(x).
questions.hint: For x ≠ 1, f(x) simplifies to x + 1.
questions.explanation: f(x) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1) = x + 1 for x ≠ 1, so the values are 1.9, 1.99, 2.01, 2.1. They approach 2 from both sides, so the limit is 2.

questions.q: Match each limit to its value.
questions.hint: Factor numerator and denominator, cancel, then substitute.

questions.q: Find the intervals on which f(x) = ln x/(x² − 5x + 6) is continuous. Write your answer as a union of intervals.
questions.hint: ln x needs x > 0, and the denominator cannot be 0.
questions.explanation: ln x requires x > 0. x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 when x = 2 or x = 3. So f is continuous on (0, 2) ∪ (2, 3) ∪ (3, ∞).

questions.q: On which set is g(x) = √(x − 1)/(x² − 16) continuous?
questions.hint: The square root needs x − 1 ≥ 0; the denominator is 0 at x = ±4.
questions.explanation: √(x − 1) needs x ≥ 1 (x = 1 is allowed). x² − 16 = 0 at x = 4 and x = −4, but −4 is already excluded. So g is continuous on [1, 4) ∪ (4, ∞).

questions.q: Match each function to the set on which it is continuous.
questions.hint: Find where each function is undefined.
questions.explanation: ln(x − 2) needs x > 2. 1/(x² − 9) is undefined at x = ±3. √(5 − x) needs x ≤ 5. x² + 1 is never 0, so eˣ/(x² + 1) is continuous everywhere.

questions.q: h(x) = ln(x + 3)/(x − 1). Complete each blank.
questions.hint: Combine the domain of the log with the zero of the denominator.
questions.explanation: ln(x + 3) needs x + 3 > 0, so x > −3. The denominator is 0 at x = 1. Therefore h is continuous on (−3, 1) ∪ (1, ∞).

questions.q: Find the intervals on which f(x) = (x + 2)/(x² + 9) is continuous.
questions.hint: Can x² + 9 ever equal 0?
questions.explanation: x² ≥ 0, so x² + 9 ≥ 9 > 0 for every real x. The denominator is never zero, so f is continuous on (−∞, ∞).

questions.q: Find the intervals on which f(x) = e^(2x)/(x² − 25) is continuous.
questions.hint: e^(2x) is continuous everywhere; check the denominator.
questions.explanation: x² − 25 = (x − 5)(x + 5) = 0 at x = 5 and x = −5. Removing both gives (−∞, −5) ∪ (−5, 5) ∪ (5, ∞).

questions.q: For each function, list the x-values where it is NOT continuous (type 'none' if it is continuous everywhere).
questions.hint: Set each denominator equal to 0 and look for real solutions.
questions.explanation: x² + 1 is never 0. x² − 4x = x(x − 4) = 0 at x = 0 and x = 4. x + 7 = 0 at x = −7. x² + 2x + 5 has discriminant 4 − 20 = −16 < 0, so it is never 0.

questions.q: f(x) = 4 cos x for x < 0, f(0) = 2k, and f(x) = (a sin x)/x for x > 0. Find a and k so that f is continuous everywhere.
questions.hint: Use cos 0 = 1 and sin x/x → 1 as x → 0.
questions.explanation: Left-hand limit: 4 cos 0 = 4. Right-hand limit: a · 1 = a. For continuity both equal f(0) = 2k, so a = 4 and 2k = 4, giving k = 2.

questions.q: f(x) = x² + a for x < 1, f(1) = 5, and f(x) = bx + 1 for x > 1. Find a and b so that f is continuous at x = 1.
questions.hint: Both one-sided limits must equal f(1) = 5.
questions.explanation: Left: 1 + a = 5, so a = 4. Right: b(1) + 1 = 5, so b = 4.

questions.q: f(x) = kx + 3 for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = x² + 5 for x > 2. Find k so that f is continuous everywhere.
questions.hint: Match the two pieces at x = 2.
questions.explanation: Left value: 2k + 3. Right limit: 2² + 5 = 9. Setting 2k + 3 = 9 gives k = 3.

questions.q: f(x) = sin(3x)/x for x < 0, f(0) = c, and f(x) = x + d for x > 0. Find c and d so that f is continuous at 0.
questions.hint: sin(3x)/x = 3 · sin(3x)/(3x).
questions.explanation: The left-hand limit is 3 · 1 = 3. The right-hand limit is 0 + d = d. For continuity, c = 3 and d = 3.

questions.q: By the Intermediate Value Theorem, f(x) = x³ − 2x − 5 has a zero in which interval?
questions.hint: Look for a sign change in f between the endpoints.
questions.explanation: f(2) = 8 − 4 − 5 = −1 and f(3) = 27 − 6 − 5 = 16. f is continuous and changes sign on [2, 3], so it has a zero there. On the other intervals f stays negative: f(−1) = −4, f(0) = −5, f(1) = −6.

questions.q: Complete the table for f(x) = x³ − 3x + 1. (Sign changes show where the IVT guarantees zeros.)
questions.hint: Substitute each x carefully, watching signs.
questions.explanation: f(−2) = −8 + 6 + 1 = −1, f(−1) = −1 + 3 + 1 = 3, f(1) = 1 − 3 + 1 = −1, f(2) = 8 − 6 + 1 = 3. The signs change on [−2, −1], [0, 1] and [1, 2], so f has a zero in each of these intervals.

questions.q: Use the IVT for f(x) = x² − 3 on [1, 2].

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The exact zero in [1, 2] is x =

questions.hint: A sign change on a continuous function guarantees a zero.
questions.explanation: f(1) = 1 − 3 = −2 and f(2) = 4 − 3 = 1. The sign changes, so there is a zero in [1, 2]. Solving x² = 3 gives x = √3 ≈ 1.73, which is in the interval.

questions.q: Each function is continuous and increasing, so it has exactly one zero. Match each function to the interval that contains its zero.
questions.hint: Evaluate at the integer endpoints and look for a sign change.

questions.q: Using the Intermediate Value Theorem, the function f(x) = x³ + 3x − 5 has a zero in which interval?
questions.hint: Evaluate f at both endpoints of each interval and look for a sign change.
questions.explanation: f is a polynomial, so it is continuous. f(1) = 1 + 3 − 5 = −1 < 0 and f(2) = 8 + 6 − 5 = 9 > 0. The sign changes on [1, 2], so by the IVT f has a zero there.
