parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Remainder when p(x) is divided by x − 2:

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Is x − 2 a factor of p(x)? (yes/no)

questions.hint: Evaluate p(−1) and p(2).
questions.explanation: p(−1) = 0·(8) − 6 = −6. p(2) = (3)(4 − 6 + 4) − 6 = 3·2 − 6 = 0. Since the remainder is 0, x − 2 is a factor of p(x).

questions.q: Let f(x) = 3x³ − 4x² + x + 2. Which of the following is NOT a possible rational root of f?
questions.hint: Possible rational roots are ± (factors of 2) / (factors of 3).
questions.explanation: p is a factor of 2: 1, 2; q is a factor of 3: 1, 3. The possible roots are ±1, ±2, ±1/3, ±2/3. 3/2 would need 3 to divide the constant 2 and 2 to divide the leading 3, so it is not on the list.

questions.q: Let f(x) = 4x³ + x − 6. Which of the following is NOT a possible rational zero of f?
questions.hint: The numerator must divide 6 and the denominator must divide 4.
questions.explanation: Numerators: 1, 2, 3, 6. Denominators: 1, 2, 4. 3/4, −3/2 and 6 all fit. 2/3 has denominator 3, which does not divide 4, so it is not possible.

questions.q: For f(x) = 2x⁴ − x + 5, decide whether each value is a POSSIBLE rational zero (by the Rational Zeros Theorem). Write yes or no.
questions.hint: List ± (factors of 5) / (factors of 2).
questions.explanation: p ∈ {1, 5} and q ∈ {1, 2}, so the possible rational zeros are ±1, ±5, ±1/2, ±5/2. So 5, −5/2 and −1/2 are possible; 2 and 1/5 are not.

questions.q: How many possible rational zeros (counting + and − separately) does the Rational Zeros Theorem give for f(x) = 2x³ + 3x − 9?
questions.hint: Find all p/q with p dividing 9 and q dividing 2, then count with ±.
questions.explanation: p ∈ {1, 3, 9} and q ∈ {1, 2} give 1, 3, 9, 1/2, 3/2, 9/2. With ± that is 6 × 2 = 12 possible rational zeros.

questions.q: Which binomial is a factor of x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6?
questions.hint: Test x − a by checking whether f(a) = 0.
questions.explanation: f(1) = 1 − 2 − 5 + 6 = 0, so x − 1 is a factor. Checking the others: f(−1) = 8, f(2) = −4, f(−3) = −24, none zero.

questions.q: Which binomial is a factor of x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6?
questions.hint: For x + 3, evaluate f(−3).
questions.explanation: f(−3) = −27 + 18 + 15 − 6 = 0, so x + 3 is a factor. f(1) = −8, f(−2) = 4 and f(3) = 24, so the others are not factors.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x³ + 3x² − 4. Complete the table to decide which binomials are factors.
questions.hint: Substitute the tested value into f(x); a result of 0 means a factor.

questions.q: Which is NOT a factor of x³ + 2x² − 3x?
questions.hint: Factor out x first, then factor the quadratic.
questions.explanation: x³ + 2x² − 3x = x(x² + 2x − 3) = x(x + 3)(x − 1). So x, x + 3 and x − 1 are factors, but x + 1 is not.

questions.q: Which is NOT a factor of x⁴ − 5x² + 4?
questions.hint: Treat it as a quadratic in x²: (x² − 1)(x² − 4).

questions.q: Factor 2x³ − 8x completely.
questions.hint: Take out 2x, then use a difference of squares.
questions.explanation: 2x³ − 8x = 2x(x² − 4) = 2x(x − 2)(x + 2). Setting each factor to zero gives x = 0, 2 and −2.

questions.q: Match each polynomial with its complete factorization.
questions.hint: Factor out x, then find two numbers with the right product and sum.
questions.explanation: x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2); x² + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2); x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3); x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3). Each polynomial is x times that quadratic.

questions.q: What is the remainder when f(x) = x⁴ + 1 is divided by x + 1?
questions.hint: By the Remainder Theorem the remainder is f(−1).
questions.explanation: f(−1) = (−1)⁴ + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2. The expression x³ − x² + x − 1 is the quotient, not the remainder.

questions.q: What is the remainder when x⁷ − 3 is divided by x − 1?
questions.hint: Evaluate the polynomial at x = 1.
questions.explanation: By the Remainder Theorem the remainder is f(1) = 1⁷ − 3 = 1 − 3 = −2.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x⁵ − 2. Use the Remainder Theorem to find the remainder for each divisor.
questions.hint: For x − a use f(a); for x + a use f(−a). An odd power keeps the sign.

questions.hint: Use ± (factors of the constant −3) / (factors of the leading coefficient 2).
questions.explanation: p ∈ {1, 3} and q ∈ {1, 2}. The quotients p/q are 1, 3, 1/2, 3/2, so the possible rational zeros are ±1, ±3, ±1/2, ±3/2.

questions.q: For f(x) = 3x³ − 2x² + 7x + 4, the factors of the constant are p = 1, 2, 4 and the factors of the leading coefficient are q = 1, 3. Complete the table of p/q values (positive values only).
questions.hint: Divide each p by 1 and by 3.
questions.explanation: 1/3, 2/1 = 2, 2/3, 4/1 = 4 and 4/3. With signs, the possible rational zeros are ±1, ±2, ±4, ±1/3, ±2/3, ±4/3.

questions.q: Which is the set of possible rational zeros of f(x) = x⁴ − 3x² + 6?
questions.hint: The leading coefficient is 1, so q can only be ±1.
questions.explanation: p must divide 6: 1, 2, 3, 6. q must divide 1. So the possible rational zeros are ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6.

questions.q: Complete the synthetic division of 2x⁴ − 5x³ + 4x − 7 by x − 2. (Note the x² coefficient is 0.)
questions.hint: Bring down the 2, multiply by 2, add to the next coefficient, and repeat.
questions.explanation: Bring down 2. 2·2 = 4, −5 + 4 = −1. −1·2 = −2, 0 − 2 = −2. −2·2 = −4, 4 − 4 = 0. 0·2 = 0, −7 + 0 = −7. So the quotient is 2x³ − x² − 2x + 0 and the remainder is −7.

questions.q: Use synthetic division to find the quotient of (x³ + 2x² − 13x + 10) ÷ (x − 2).
questions.hint: Use 2 in the synthetic division box.
questions.explanation: Coefficients 1, 2, −13, 10 with 2: bring down 1; 2 + 2 = 4; −13 + 8 = −5; 10 − 10 = 0. The quotient is x² + 4x − 5 with remainder 0.

questions.q: Use synthetic division to divide 3x³ − 7x² + 5 by x − 3.
questions.hint: Include a 0 for the missing x term: 3, −7, 0, 5.
questions.explanation: With 3: bring down 3; −7 + 9 = 2; 0 + 6 = 6; 5 + 18 = 23. The quotient is 3x² + 2x + 6 and the remainder is 23.

questions.q: When x⁴ − 3x³ + 2x − 5 is divided by x + 1 using synthetic division, what is the bottom row?
questions.hint: Use −1 in the box and remember the 0 for the missing x² term.
questions.explanation: Coefficients 1, −3, 0, 2, −5 with −1: bring down 1; −3 − 1 = −4; 0 + 4 = 4; 2 − 4 = −2; −5 + 2 = −3. So the quotient is x³ − 4x² + 4x − 2 and the remainder is −3.

questions.q: Use long division to divide x⁴ + 2x³ − x + 3 by x² + x − 1.
questions.hint: Write the dividend as x⁴ + 2x³ + 0x² − x + 3 and divide by the leading term x².
questions.explanation: x⁴ ÷ x² = x²; subtract x⁴ + x³ − x² to get x³ + x² − x + 3. x³ ÷ x² = x; subtract x³ + x² − x to get 3. So the quotient is x² + x and the remainder is 3.

questions.q: Which summary statement is correct for dividing 2x³ + 3x² − x + 4 by x² + 1?
questions.hint: Divide 2x³ by x² first, subtract, then divide again.
questions.explanation: 2x³ ÷ x² = 2x; subtract 2x³ + 2x to get 3x² − 3x + 4. 3x² ÷ x² = 3; subtract 3x² + 3 to get −3x + 1. Check: (x² + 1)(2x + 3) = 2x³ + 3x² + 2x + 3, and adding −3x + 1 gives 2x³ + 3x² − x + 4.

questions.q: Use long division to write (x³ − 4x² + 5) ÷ (x² − 2) in fraction form: quotient + remainder/divisor.
questions.hint: Use 0x for the missing term: x³ − 4x² + 0x + 5.
questions.explanation: x³ ÷ x² = x; subtract x³ − 2x to get −4x² + 2x + 5. −4x² ÷ x² = −4; subtract −4x² + 8 to get 2x − 3. So the result is x − 4 + (2x − 3)/(x² − 2).

questions.q: Simplify (6x³ − x² − 5x + 2)/(2x − 1) using synthetic or long division.
questions.hint: Divide by x − 1/2 with synthetic division, then divide the quotient by 2.
questions.explanation: With 1/2: bring down 6; −1 + 3 = 2; −5 + 1 = −4; 2 − 2 = 0. So the dividend = (x − 1/2)(6x² + 2x − 4) = (2x − 1)(3x² + x − 2). The answer is 3x² + x − 2.

questions.q: Simplify (4x³ + 8x² − x − 2)/(2x + 1).
questions.hint: Synthetic division by −1/2 gives the quotient for x + 1/2; divide it by 2 for 2x + 1.
questions.explanation: With −1/2: bring down 4; 8 − 2 = 6; −1 − 3 = −4; −2 + 2 = 0. So the dividend = (x + 1/2)(4x² + 6x − 4) = (2x + 1)(2x² + 3x − 2). Forgetting to divide by 2 gives 4x² + 6x − 4.

questions.q: To divide 2x³ − x² − 5x + 3 by 2x − 3, use synthetic division with 3/2. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Bring down 2, multiply by 3/2, add, and repeat.

questions.q: Simplify (3x³ + 4x² − 5x − 2)/(3x + 1), then factor the dividend completely.
questions.hint: Use −1/3 in synthetic division, then divide the quotient by 3.
questions.explanation: With −1/3: bring down 3; 4 − 1 = 3; −5 − 1 = −6; −2 + 2 = 0. The bottom row 3, 3, −6 divided by 3 gives x² + x − 2 = (x + 2)(x − 1). So 3x³ + 4x² − 5x − 2 = (3x + 1)(x + 2)(x − 1).

questions.q: Use the Factor Theorem to decide whether (x − 3) is a factor of x³ − 4x² + x + 6.
questions.hint: x − 3 is a factor exactly when f(3) = 0.
questions.explanation: f(3) = 27 − 36 + 3 + 6 = 0. By the Factor Theorem, x − 3 is a factor.

questions.q: Is (x + 2) a factor of x³ + x² − 4x + 4?
questions.hint: For x + 2, the value to test is x = −2.
questions.explanation: f(−2) = −8 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 8 ≠ 0, so x + 2 is not a factor. Testing f(2) checks x − 2, not x + 2.

questions.q: Use the Factor Theorem to complete the table.
questions.hint: For x − a evaluate at a; for x + a evaluate at −a.

questions.q: Determine whether t − 2 is a factor of 2t⁴ − 3t³ − 5t² + 3t + 6.
questions.hint: Substitute t = 2.

questions.q: Is t + 3 a factor of t⁴ + 2t³ − 4t² − 5t − 6?
questions.hint: Test t = −3 for the factor t + 3.
questions.explanation: f(−3) = 81 − 54 − 36 + 15 − 6 = 0, so t + 3 is a factor. f(3) = 78 is true but it tests t − 3, not t + 3.

questions.q: Find the remainder when 3t⁴ − t³ + 2t − 8 is divided by t + 2. (Then decide for yourself: is t + 2 a factor?)
questions.hint: Evaluate f(−2).

right: remainder 0, so it is a factor

questions.q: For f(x) = 4x³ − 3x − 1, use the Rational Zeros Theorem.
questions.hint: Candidates are ± (factors of 1) / (factors of 4); test x = 1 first.
questions.explanation: The candidates are ±1, ±1/2, ±1/4. f(1) = 4 − 3 − 1 = 0, and dividing gives 4x² + 4x + 1 = (2x + 1)², so x = −1/2 is also a zero. The rational zeros are 1 and −1/2.

questions.q: Which of the following is a zero of f(x) = 3x³ − x² − 3x + 1?
questions.hint: All four values are on the candidate list; substitute each or factor by grouping.
questions.explanation: By grouping, f(x) = x²(3x − 1) − (3x − 1) = (3x − 1)(x − 1)(x + 1). So the zeros are 1/3, 1 and −1; of the choices only 1/3 works.

questions.q: For f(x) = 2x³ + x² − 2x − 1, test some potential rational zeros. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully; with fractions, (1/2)³ = 1/8.

questions.q: Use the Rational Zeros Theorem for f(x) = 2x³ + x − 3.
questions.hint: Divide factors of 3 by factors of 2, then test the simplest values first.
questions.explanation: p ∈ {1, 3}, q ∈ {1, 2} give ±1, ±3, ±1/2, ±3/2. f(1) = 2 + 1 − 3 = 0, and f(x) = (x − 1)(2x² + 2x + 3). The quadratic has discriminant 4 − 24 < 0, so 1 is the only rational zero.

questions.q: Which list gives all potential rational zeros of f(x) = 3x³ + 2x − 5?
questions.hint: p comes from the constant (5) and q from the leading coefficient (3).
questions.explanation: p ∈ {1, 5} and q ∈ {1, 3}, so p/q gives ±1, ±5, ±1/3, ±5/3. Swapping p and q gives the wrong list ±1, ±3, ±1/5, ±3/5.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x³ − x² + 2x − 1 has exactly one rational zero. Find it. Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.hint: Try grouping the first two terms and the last two terms.
questions.explanation: f(x) = x²(2x − 1) + 1(2x − 1) = (2x − 1)(x² + 1). x² + 1 has no real zeros, so the only rational zero is x = 1/2.

questions.q: Each polynomial has exactly one rational zero. Match each polynomial with it.
questions.hint: Test candidates from the Rational Zeros Theorem, or factor by grouping.

questions.q: For f(x) = x³ − 3x² − 2x + 4: (i) list the possible rational zeros, (ii) find the rational zero, (iii) find the other two zeros.
questions.hint: Test x = 1, divide, and use the quadratic formula on what is left.
questions.explanation: Candidates are ±1, ±2, ±4. f(1) = 1 − 3 − 2 + 4 = 0. Synthetic division by 1 gives x² − 2x − 4, and x = (2 ± √20)/2 = 1 ± √5.

questions.q: f(x) = x³ + x² − 7x − 3 has the zero x = −3. Complete the synthetic division by x + 3.
questions.hint: Bring down 1, multiply by −3, add, and repeat.

questions.q: Find all the zeros of f(x) = x³ − 6x − 4.
questions.hint: The possible rational zeros are ±1, ±2, ±4; try x = −2.
questions.explanation: f(−2) = −8 + 12 − 4 = 0. Synthetic division of 1, 0, −6, −4 by −2 gives 1, −2, −2, remainder 0, so the quotient is x² − 2x − 2. Then x = (2 ± √12)/2 = 1 ± √3.

questions.q: Given that x = 1 is a zero of f(x) = x³ − 4x² + x + 2, find the other two zeros.
questions.hint: Divide by x − 1 and use the quadratic formula.
questions.explanation: Synthetic division with 1: 1, −3, −2, remainder 0. So f(x) = (x − 1)(x² − 3x − 2). The quadratic formula gives x = (3 ± √(9 + 8))/2 = (3 ± √17)/2.

questions.q: Given f(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6.
questions.hint: The leading coefficient is 1, so the candidates are the factors of 6.
questions.explanation: Candidates: ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6. f(1) = 0, and dividing gives x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2). So the zeros are −2, 1, 3 and f(x) = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3).

questions.q: What are all the zeros of f(x) = x³ − 7x − 6?
questions.hint: Test the factors of 6; f(−1) is a good start.
questions.explanation: f(−1) = −1 + 7 − 6 = 0. Dividing by x + 1 gives x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2). So the zeros are −1, −2 and 3.

questions.q: For f(x) = x³ − 4x² − 7x + 10, test some possible rational zeros. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Substitute each value; a degree-3 polynomial has at most 3 zeros.

questions.q: f(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6 has three rational zeros. Find them and plot the three x-intercepts and the y-intercept.
questions.hint: Test the factors of 6, starting with x = −1.
questions.explanation: f(−1) = −1 + 2 + 5 − 6 = 0. Dividing by x + 1 gives x² + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2). So the x-intercepts are (−3, 0), (−1, 0), (2, 0), and f(0) = −6 gives the y-intercept (0, −6).

questions.q: Find the polynomial function with leading coefficient 3, degree 3, and zeros 1/3, −2 and 1. Write it in standard form.
questions.hint: The zero 1/3 together with the leading coefficient 3 gives the factor (3x − 1).

questions.q: Which polynomial has leading coefficient 2, degree 3, and zeros −1, 3/2 and 2?
Find the polynomial with leading coefficient −1, degree 3, and zeros 0, 2 and −4.
questions.hint: A zero at 0 gives the factor x.

questions.q: Write a polynomial function of minimum degree in standard form with real coefficients whose zeros include 3 and 2i.
questions.hint: With real coefficients, −2i must also be a zero.
questions.explanation: The zeros are 3, 2i and −2i. (x − 2i)(x + 2i) = x² + 4, so f(x) = (x − 3)(x² + 4) = x³ − 3x² + 4x − 12.

questions.q: Write a polynomial function of minimum degree in standard form (leading coefficient 1) with real coefficients whose zeros include −2 and 3i.
questions.hint: Include the conjugate −3i, then multiply.
questions.explanation: The zeros are −2, 3i and −3i. (x − 3i)(x + 3i) = x² + 9. f(x) = (x + 2)(x² + 9) = x³ + 2x² + 9x + 18.

questions.q: A polynomial of minimum degree with real coefficients and leading coefficient 1 has zeros 1 and 1 + i.

questions.explanation: Complex zeros come in conjugate pairs, so 1 − i is a zero. (x − 1)² + 1 = x² − 2x + 2. Then (x − 1)(x² − 2x + 2) = x³ − 3x² + 4x − 2.

questions.q: Each set of zeros belongs to a minimum-degree polynomial with real coefficients and leading coefficient 1. Match each set to its polynomial.
questions.hint: i pairs with −i to give x² + 1; 2i pairs with −2i to give x² + 4.
questions.explanation: (x − 2)(x² + 1) = x³ − 2x² + x − 2. (x + 2)(x² + 1) = x³ + 2x² + x + 2. (x − 2)(x² + 4) = x³ − 2x² + 4x − 8. (x + 2)(x² + 4) = x³ + 2x² + 4x + 8. The extra option is (x − 2)(x² − 1), which has only real zeros.

questions.q: Which of the following cannot be the number of nonreal zeros of a polynomial of degree 6 with real coefficients?
questions.hint: Nonreal zeros of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs.
questions.explanation: Nonreal zeros appear in pairs a + bi and a − bi, so their number is even. A degree-6 polynomial can have 0, 2, 4 or 6 nonreal zeros, but never 5.

questions.q: A polynomial of degree 3 with real coefficients has 2 + i as a zero. How many real zeros does it have (counting multiplicity)?
questions.hint: If 2 + i is a zero, so is its conjugate.
questions.explanation: 2 − i must also be a zero, which uses 2 of the 3 zeros. The remaining zero must be real (it has no partner), so there is exactly 1 real zero.

questions.q: For a polynomial with real coefficients, list every possible number of nonreal zeros (counting multiplicity). Complete the table.
questions.hint: The count must be even and at most the degree.
questions.explanation: Nonreal zeros come in conjugate pairs, so the count is even. Degree 2: 0 or 2. Degree 3: 0 or 2 (at least one zero is real). Degree 4: 0, 2 or 4.

questions.q: A polynomial of degree 7 with real coefficients has exactly 3 real zeros (counting multiplicity). How many nonreal zeros does it have?
questions.hint: A degree-7 polynomial has 7 zeros in total, counting multiplicity.
questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra there are 7 zeros in all. 7 − 3 = 4 nonreal zeros, which is even, as conjugate pairs require.

questions.q: Which polynomial has the complex roots 2 + i√3 and 2 − i√3?
questions.hint: Multiply (x − 2 − i√3)(x − 2 + i√3) as a difference of squares.
questions.explanation: (x − 2)² − (i√3)² = x² − 4x + 4 − (−3) = x² − 4x + 7. Forgetting i² = −1 gives x² − 4x + 1.

questions.q: Write the quadratic polynomial (leading coefficient 1) whose roots are −1 + 2i and −1 − 2i. Give it in standard form.
questions.hint: Use (x + 1)² − (2i)².

questions.q: Match each pair of complex roots with its quadratic polynomial (leading coefficient 1).
questions.hint: For roots a ± bi the polynomial is (x − a)² + b².

questions.q: A quadratic with leading coefficient 1 has roots 4 + i√5 and 4 − i√5.
questions.hint: The product (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b².
questions.explanation: Sum: (4 + i√5) + (4 − i√5) = 8. Product: 4² + (√5)² = 16 + 5 = 21. So the polynomial is x² − 8x + 21.

questions.q: Let z = 2 + 5i and z̄ its complex conjugate. Which of the following is NOT a real number?
questions.hint: Compute each one: z̄ = 2 − 5i.
questions.explanation: z + z̄ = 4 and z·z̄ = 4 + 25 = 29 are real. z − z̄ = 10i is not real. (z − z̄)² = (10i)² = −100 is real.

questions.q: Let z = 4 − 3i.
questions.hint: Remember i² = −1 when multiplying.

questions.q: Complete the table for each complex number z.
questions.hint: For z = a + bi: z̄ = a − bi, z + z̄ = 2a and z·z̄ = a² + b².
questions.explanation: 3 + 2i: conjugate 3 − 2i, sum 6, product 9 + 4 = 13. −1 − 4i: conjugate −1 + 4i, sum −2, product 1 + 16 = 17. 5i: conjugate −5i, sum 0, product 25.

questions.q: Let z = 1 + 2i. Find z² in the form a + bi.
questions.hint: Expand (1 + 2i)(1 + 2i) and use i² = −1.
questions.explanation: z² = 1 + 4i + 4i² = 1 + 4i − 4 = −3 + 4i. It is not a real number.

questions.q: Which is the expression (2 − 5i)(1 + 3i) in the form a + bi?
questions.hint: Use FOIL, then replace i² with −1.
questions.explanation: (2 − 5i)(1 + 3i) = 2 + 6i − 5i − 15i² = 2 + i + 15 = 17 + i. Treating i² as +1 gives −13 + i.

questions.q: Write (−4 + i)(2 − 3i) in the form a + bi.
questions.hint: Multiply all four pairs of terms, then use i² = −1.

questions.q: Write each product in the form a + bi.
questions.hint: Use i² = −1; conjugate products give a² + b².

questions.q: Match each expression with its value in a + bi form.
questions.hint: Expand and replace i² with −1; i³ = i²·i.
(x − 2i)(x + 2i) = x² − 4i² = x² + 4.
questions.explanation: (x − 2i)(x + 2i) = x² + 4, so f(x) = (x + 3)(x² + 4) = x³ + 3x² + 4x + 12. The real zero is −3 and the nonreal zeros are ±2i. Only real zeros give x-intercepts, so the only x-intercept is (−3, 0).

questions.q: How many x-intercepts does the graph of f(x) = (x − 1)(x − 4)(x² + 9) have?
questions.hint: Only real zeros show up as x-intercepts.
questions.explanation: The zeros are 1, 4, 3i and −3i (since x² + 9 = 0 gives x = ±3i). The nonreal zeros ±3i are not on the x-axis, so the graph has 2 x-intercepts, at x = 1 and x = 4.

questions.q: Plot all the x-intercepts and the y-intercept of f(x) = (x + 4)(x − 1)(x² + 1).
questions.hint: x² + 1 has no real zeros, so it gives no x-intercepts.
questions.explanation: The real zeros are −4 and 1, giving x-intercepts (−4, 0) and (1, 0); x² + 1 = 0 gives ±i, which are not on the graph. f(0) = (4)(−1)(1) = −4, so the y-intercept is (0, −4).

questions.q: For f(x) = (x − 2)(x² + 5), the zeros are 2, √5 i and −√5 i. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Only real zeros are x-intercepts.
questions.explanation: x = 2 is real, so (2, 0) is an x-intercept. x² + 5 = 0 gives x = ±√5 i, which are nonreal, so they do not give x-intercepts.

questions.q: Which polynomial function of minimum degree with real coefficients has zeros 3, −1 and 1 + 2i?
questions.hint: Complex zeros of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs, so 1 − 2i is also a zero.
questions.explanation: The zeros are 3, −1, 1 + 2i and 1 − 2i. (x − 3)(x + 1) = x² − 2x − 3 and (x − 1 − 2i)(x − 1 + 2i) = (x − 1)² + 4 = x² − 2x + 5. Multiplying: (x² − 2x − 3)(x² − 2x + 5) = x⁴ − 4x³ + 6x² − 4x − 15.

questions.q: Write a polynomial function of minimum degree in standard form with real coefficients whose zeros include 2 and 3i. Use leading coefficient 1.
questions.hint: Include the conjugate −3i, then multiply the factors.
questions.explanation: Because 3i is a zero, −3i is also a zero, and (x − 3i)(x + 3i) = x² + 9. Multiply by (x − 2): (x − 2)(x² + 9) = x³ − 2x² + 9x − 18.

questions.q: A polynomial f of minimum degree with real coefficients and leading coefficient 1 has zeros 1, −2 and 3 + i. Complete the following.
