questions.hint: The angle of depression equals the angle of elevation at the bus, so tan θ = 120 / distance.

questions.q: Layla is on a small boat and her eye level is 5 feet above the water. She sees a buoy floating on the water at an angle of depression of 4°. What is the line-of-sight distance from her eyes to the buoy? Round to the nearest foot.
questions.hint: The 5 ft height is opposite the angle at the buoy, and the line of sight is the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: The angle at the buoy equals the angle of depression, 4°. sin 4° = 5/d, so d = 5/sin 4° ≈ 71.7 ≈ 72 ft.

questions.q: A fisherman's eye level is 4 feet above the surface of a lake. He sees a float on the water at an angle of depression of 15°. What is the horizontal distance from the fisherman to the float, to the nearest tenth of a foot?
questions.hint: Horizontal distance is adjacent to the angle and the 4 ft height is opposite it.
questions.explanation: tan 15° = 4/d, so d = 4/tan 15° ≈ 14.9 ft. Using sin gives the slanted line of sight (15.5 ft), not the horizontal distance.

questions.q: A lifeguard's eyes are 3 m above the water. Match each angle of depression to a swimmer with the line-of-sight distance from the lifeguard's eyes to that swimmer (rounded to the nearest tenth).
questions.hint: Line of sight = 3 / sin(angle of depression).
questions.explanation: d = 3/sin θ: 10° → 17.3 m, 20° → 8.8 m, 30° → 3/0.5 = 6.0 m, 45° → 4.2 m. The value 17.0 m is the horizontal distance for 10°, not the line of sight.

questions.q: In triangle PQR, PQ = 6, QR = 15 and m∠Q = 118°. Which expression gives the area of triangle PQR?
questions.hint: Area = ½ × (side) × (side) × sin(included angle).
questions.explanation: The angle Q is between sides PQ and QR, so Area = ½ · 6 · 15 · sin 118° = 45 sin 118°. 90 sin 118° forgets the ½, and cos is the wrong ratio.

questions.q: Match each triangle to the expression for its area.
questions.hint: Halve the product of the two sides, then multiply by the sine of the angle between them.

questions.q: In triangle KLM, KL = 10 cm, LM = 7 cm and m∠L = 150°. Find the exact area of the triangle in cm².
questions.hint: sin 150° = ½.

questions.q: In triangle DEF, DE = 6.2, DF = 8.5 and m∠D = 45°. Find the area of the triangle. Round to the nearest tenth of a square unit.
questions.hint: Angle D is between sides DE and DF, so use Area = ½·DE·DF·sin D.

questions.q: Each row gives two sides of a triangle and the angle between them. Complete the area column, rounding to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Area = ½ × side 1 × side 2 × sin(included angle).

questions.q: An acute triangle has two sides of length 10 cm and 12 cm and an area of 40 cm². What is the measure of the angle between those two sides, to the nearest tenth of a degree?
questions.hint: Set ½·10·12·sin θ = 40 and solve for sin θ.
questions.explanation: 60 sin θ = 40, so sin θ = 2/3 and θ = sin⁻¹(2/3) ≈ 41.8°. The angle 138.2° also has sine 2/3 but is obtuse.

questions.q: A flagpole casts a shadow 25 m long when the angle of elevation of the sun is 38°. Find the height of the flagpole to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: The height is opposite the 38° angle and the shadow is adjacent to it.
questions.explanation: tan 38° = h/25, so h = 25 tan 38° ≈ 19.5 ≈ 20 m. Using sin gives 15 m and dividing by tan gives 32 m.

questions.q: A tree is 12 m tall. When the angle of elevation of the sun is 50°, how long is the tree's shadow? Round to the nearest tenth of a metre.
questions.hint: tan 50° = height ÷ shadow length.

questions.q: A building's shadow is 17 ft long. Complete the table of the building's height for different angles of elevation of the sun. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
questions.hint: Height = 17 × tan(angle of elevation).

questions.q: A 40 m tower casts a 30 m shadow. What is the angle of elevation of the sun, to the nearest degree?
questions.hint: Use the inverse tangent: tan θ = opposite/adjacent.

questions.q: From the top of a 150 ft lighthouse, a keeper sees a sailboat at an angle of depression of 24°. How far is the sailboat from the base of the lighthouse? Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
questions.hint: At the boat, the angle of elevation is 24° and the 150 ft height is opposite it.
questions.explanation: tan 24° = 150/d, so d = 150/tan 24° ≈ 336.9 ft. 150/sin 24° is the line-of-sight distance, not the distance along the ground.

questions.q: From the edge of an 85 m cliff, the angle of depression to a car parked on level ground is 32°. How far is the car from the foot of the cliff? Round to the nearest tenth of a metre.
questions.hint: Distance from the base = height ÷ tan(angle of depression).

questions.q: Each observer is at the top of a tower of the given height and sees an object on the ground at the given angle of depression. Match each to the horizontal distance from the tower's base (nearest tenth).
questions.hint: Use d = height / tan(angle) for each one.
questions.explanation: 50/tan 30° ≈ 86.6; 200/tan 45° = 200.0; 90/tan 10° ≈ 510.4; 300/tan 60° ≈ 173.2. 28.9 m comes from multiplying by tan instead of dividing.

questions.q: An air traffic controller is at the top of a 90 ft tower. A plane on the runway is 300 ft from the base of the tower. What is the angle of depression from the controller to the plane, to the nearest degree?
questions.hint: tan(angle) = height ÷ horizontal distance.

questions.q: Mariam sits at the end of a pier that is 20 ft above the water. Her eyes are 5 ft above the pier. She sees a dolphin at the surface at an angle of depression of 15°. How far is the dolphin from her eyes? Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
questions.hint: First add the two heights; the total height is opposite the 15° angle and the line of sight is the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation: Total height = 20 + 5 = 25 ft. sin 15° = 25/d, so d = 25/sin 15° ≈ 96.6 ft. Forgetting the 5 ft gives 77.3 ft.

questions.q: A balcony is 45 m above the ground and Khalid's eyes are 1.5 m above the balcony floor. He sees a fountain at an angle of depression of 28°. How far is the fountain from the point directly below Khalid? Round to the nearest tenth of a metre.
questions.hint: Use the total height 46.5 m and the tangent ratio for the horizontal distance.

questions.explanation: Height = 12 + 2 = 14 m. Line of sight = 14/sin 18° ≈ 45.3 m. Horizontal distance = 14/tan 18° ≈ 43.1 m.

questions.q: Triangle ABC has a = 5, b = 7 and c = 8. Match each angle to its cosine.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 3, b = 7 and c = 5. Find the exact measure of angle B in degrees.
questions.hint: Use cos B = (a² + c² − b²)/(2ac); a negative cosine means an obtuse angle.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, m∠B = 70°, AB = 30 and BC = 45. Which expression equals AC?
questions.hint: AC is opposite angle B, so AC² = AB² + BC² − 2·AB·BC·cos B.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 8, b = 5 and m∠C = 60°. Use c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
questions.hint: cos 60° = ½.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 5, b = 3 and m∠C = 120°. Find the exact length of side c.
questions.hint: cos 120° = −½, so subtracting 2ab cos C adds ab.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, m∠A = 50°, m∠C = 75° and AB = 40. Find BC to the nearest whole number.
questions.hint: BC is opposite angle A and AB is opposite angle C.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, m∠B = 40°, m∠C = 105° and BC = 20. Find AC to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: First find angle A, which is opposite BC.
questions.explanation: A = 180° − 40° − 105° = 35°. AC is opposite B: AC/sin 40° = 20/sin 35°, so AC = 20 sin 40°/sin 35° ≈ 22.4.

questions.q: Triangle ABC has m∠A = 30°, m∠B = 45° and a = 10. Complete the table. Round sides to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Angles add to 180°, and side/sin(opposite angle) is the same for all three sides.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, m∠C = 95°, m∠B = 45° and BC = 12. Find AB to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: BC is opposite angle A, so find angle A first.
questions.explanation: A = 180° − 95° − 45° = 40°. AB is opposite C: AB/sin 95° = 12/sin 40°, so AB = 12 sin 95°/sin 40° ≈ 18.6.

questions.q: In triangle PQR, m∠P = 120°, m∠Q = 25° and PQ = 15. Find QR to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: PQ is opposite angle R; find R first.
questions.explanation: R = 180° − 120° − 25° = 35°. QR is opposite P: QR = 15 sin 120°/sin 35° ≈ 22.6. Using sin 25° instead of sin 35° matches PQ with the wrong angle.

questions.q: In triangle PQR, m∠P = 120°, m∠Q = 25° and PQ = 15. Round sides to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same ratio.

questions.q: Two sides of a triangle are 8 and 11 and the angle between them is 40°. Find the third side to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Use c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C with C = 40°.

questions.q: In triangle XYZ, XY = 4, XZ = 7 and m∠X = 62°. Find YZ to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: YZ is opposite angle X, which is between the two given sides.

questions.q: Two sides of a triangle are both 5 cm. Complete the table for the third side c for each angle C between them. Round to the nearest tenth.
Solve triangle ABC with m∠A = 70°, AB = 5.2 and AC = 7.4. Round BC to the nearest tenth and angles to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Use the Law of Cosines for BC, then find the smaller angle with the Law of Sines.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, m∠A = 95°, b = 6 and c = 4. After finding a with the Law of Cosines, what is m∠C to the nearest degree?
questions.hint: Find a first, then use sin C = c·sin A / a.

questions.q: Solve triangle ABC with m∠A = 52°, b = 9 and c = 6. Round the side to the nearest tenth and angles to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Law of Cosines for a, then Law of Sines for the angle opposite the shorter side, then subtract from 180°.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, AB = 5, BC = 6 and AC = 7. Find m∠B to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Angle B is between AB and BC and is opposite AC.

questions.q: A triangle has sides 10, 12 and 18. What is the measure of its largest angle, to the nearest degree?
questions.hint: The largest angle is opposite the longest side.
questions.explanation: cos θ = (10² + 12² − 18²)/(2·10·12) = −80/240 = −1/3, so θ = cos⁻¹(−1/3) ≈ 109.5° ≈ 109°. 71° comes from dropping the negative sign.

questions.q: A triangle has sides 6, 8 and 10. Match each side with the angle opposite it (nearest degree).
questions.hint: Use the Law of Cosines for each angle; the side opposite the 10 tells you if it is a right angle.

questions.q: A triangle has sides 9, 10 and 17. Find the smallest angle to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: The smallest angle is opposite the shortest side, 9.

questions.q: Two coast-guard stations P and Q are 500 m apart. A boat B is spotted so that m∠BPQ = 52° and m∠BQP = 63°. How far is the boat from station Q? Round to the nearest tenth of a metre.
questions.hint: Find the angle at the boat first; QB is opposite the 52° angle at P.

questions.q: A surveyor marks points A and B 120 m apart on one bank of a river. A tree T is on the other bank, with m∠TAB = 70° and m∠TBA = 48°. How far is the tree from A, to the nearest metre?
questions.hint: AT is opposite the angle at B.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 4 cm, b = 6 cm and m∠C = 50°. Give c to the nearest tenth of a cm and angles to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Law of Cosines for c, then Law of Sines for the angle opposite the shorter side a.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 3 cm, b = 5 cm and m∠C = 80°. Find c to the nearest cm.
questions.hint: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, then take the square root.
questions.explanation: c² = 9 + 25 − 30 cos 80° ≈ 34 − 5.21 = 28.79, so c ≈ 5.37 ≈ 5 cm. 8 cm just adds the sides, and 29 forgets the square root.

questions.q: Solve triangle ABC with a = 5 cm, b = 8 cm and m∠C = 65°. Give the side to the nearest cm and the angles to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Find c with the Law of Cosines first.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 9 cm, b = 12 cm and m∠C = 58°. Round each answer to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Two sides and the included angle: Law of Cosines first, then Law of Sines.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 6 cm, b = 11 cm and m∠C = 40°. Find c to the nearest tenth of a cm.
questions.hint: Use c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 6 cm, b = 11 cm, m∠C = 40° and c ≈ 7.5 cm. Find m∠A to the nearest tenth of a degree.
questions.hint: sin A = a·sin C / c, and A is opposite the shortest side so it is acute.
questions.explanation: sin A = 6 sin 40°/7.5 ≈ 0.5159, so A ≈ 31.1°. Dividing by b instead of c gives the wrong value 20.5°.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, a = 8 cm, b = 11 cm and c = 13 cm. Find each angle to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: Use the Law of Cosines with the side opposite each angle in the numerator's subtracted term.

questions.q: Triangle PQR has sides p = 7, q = 9 and r = 12 (each side is opposite the angle with the same letter). Complete the table of angles to the nearest degree.
questions.hint: cos Q = (p² + r² − q²)/(2pr).

questions.q: Triangle DEF has DE = 15, EF = 9 and DF = 20. Which angle is the largest, and what is its measure to the nearest degree?
questions.hint: The largest angle is opposite the longest side DF.

questions.q: To find the distance across a pond from A to B, Noura picks a point C that is 640 m from A and 230 m from B. She measures m∠ACB = 72°. Find AB to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: AB is opposite the 72° angle at C, so use the Law of Cosines.

questions.q: Two roads leave a junction at an angle of 115°. Car 1 drives 420 m along one road and car 2 drives 380 m along the other. How far apart are the cars, to the nearest metre?
questions.hint: Use the Law of Cosines with the 115° angle; cos 115° is negative.
questions.explanation: d² = 420² + 380² − 2·420·380·cos 115° ≈ 455,700, so d ≈ 675 m. Using 65° or ignoring the angle gives the other values.

questions.q: A tunnel will run straight through a hill from P to Q. From a point R, RP = 300 m, RQ = 450 m and m∠PRQ = 50°. Round PQ to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: PQ² = RP² + RQ² − 2·RP·RQ·cos R.

questions.q: Two rangers at A and B are 30 km apart on an east-west road (A is west of B). Ranger A sees a fire at F on a bearing 40° east of north; ranger B sees it 45° west of north. Round to the nearest tenth of a km.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distance from the fire to the road (km):

questions.hint: Interior angles at A and B are 90° minus each bearing.

questions.q: Points A and B lie on an east-west road with A to the west. An object C to the north is sighted from both. Match each bearing to the interior angle of triangle ABC at that point.
questions.hint: The road runs east-west, so the interior angle = 90° − bearing from north.
questions.explanation: 90° − 25° = 65°, 90° − 62° = 28°, 90° − 35° = 55°, 90° − 70° = 20°. 115° would come from adding 90° instead of subtracting.

questions.q: Two weather stations are 40 km apart on an east-west road. Station A (west) sees a storm 30° east of north; station B (east) sees it 50° west of north. What is the angle at the storm in the triangle formed?
questions.hint: Find the interior angles at A and B first.
questions.explanation: ∠A = 90° − 30° = 60° and ∠B = 90° − 50° = 40°, so the angle at the storm is 180° − 60° − 40° = 80°. Using the bearings 30° and 50° as the interior angles would wrongly give 100°.

questions.q: For the same stations (40 km apart; ∠A = 60°, ∠B = 40°, storm angle 80°), how far is the storm from the road? Round to the nearest tenth of a km.
questions.hint: Find the distance from A to the storm with the Law of Sines, then multiply by sin A.
questions.explanation: AS = 40 sin 40°/sin 80° ≈ 26.11 km. Distance to the road = AS·sin 60° ≈ 22.6 km.

questions.q: A spinner has 8 equal sections numbered 1 to 8. List the outcomes in the event "the spinner lands on a prime number". Write it as a set, e.g. {1, 2}.
questions.hint: A prime number has exactly two factors; 1 is not prime.
questions.explanation: The numbers 1 to 8 that are prime are 2, 3, 5 and 7, so the event is {2, 3, 5, 7}.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. Match each event to its set of outcomes.
questions.hint: List the numbers 1 to 6 that fit each description.
questions.explanation: Odd: {1, 3, 5}. Greater than 4: {5, 6} (4 itself is not included). Multiples of 3: {3, 6}. Factors of 4: {1, 2, 4}.

questions.q: Two coins are tossed. Which set is the event "exactly one head"?
questions.hint: List all four outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT first.
questions.explanation: The sample space is {HH, HT, TH, TT}. Exactly one head happens in HT and TH. {HH, HT, TH} is "at least one head".

questions.q: A café lets you build a breakfast from 4 kinds of bread, 3 kinds of eggs, 5 drinks and 2 fruits. How many different breakfasts with one item from each category are possible?
questions.hint: Multiply the number of choices in each category.
questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Counting Principle: 4 × 3 × 5 × 2 = 120 breakfasts.

questions.q: Hessa has 6 tops, 4 skirts, 3 headscarves and 2 pairs of shoes. How many outfits of one top, one skirt, one headscarf and one pair of shoes can she make?
questions.hint: Multiply, don't add.
questions.explanation: 6 × 4 × 3 × 2 = 144 outfits. Adding the choices (6 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 15) is a common mistake.

questions.q: Complete the table: each row lists the number of choices in each category, and the last column is the total number of different combinations with one item from each category.
questions.hint: Total = product of the numbers of choices.

questions.q: Ali is designing a game avatar. He can choose from 6 hairstyles, 7 shirts, 3 backgrounds and 12 accessories. If he chooses one of each, how many different avatars can he create?
questions.hint: Multiply the number of options in all four categories.

questions.q: A car can be ordered in 8 colours, with 3 engine types, 2 interior styles and 5 wheel designs. How many different cars can be ordered?
questions.hint: Use the Fundamental Counting Principle.
questions.explanation: 8 × 3 × 2 × 5 = 240 different cars. Adding gives 18, which counts choices instead of combinations.

questions.q: Match each menu to the number of meals with one choice from each list.
questions.hint: Multiply the three numbers for each menu.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Which set is the event "the sum is less than 5"?
questions.hint: Sums less than 5 are 2, 3 and 4; remember (1,2) and (2,1) are different outcomes.
questions.explanation: Sum 2: (1,1). Sum 3: (1,2), (2,1). Sum 4: (1,3), (2,2), (3,1). That is 6 outcomes. Pairs with a sum of 5 are not included.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Complete the table with the number of outcomes in each event.
questions.hint: List the ordered pairs for each event, counting (a, b) and (b, a) separately.

questions.q: True or false: Two fair dice are rolled. The event "sum equals 4" is {(1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1)}.
questions.hint: Check every ordered pair that adds to 4.
questions.explanation: 1 + 3, 2 + 2 and 3 + 1 are the only ways to make 4, and each ordered pair is listed once, so the statement is true.

questions.q: True or false: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. The event "heads and an even number" is {H2, H4, H6, T2}.
questions.hint: Every outcome in the event must show heads.
questions.explanation: T2 shows tails, so it does not belong. The correct event is {H2, H4, H6}, so the statement is false.

questions.q: A pizza shop offers 3 crusts, 4 sauces and several cheeses. The shop advertises 72 different pizzas with one crust, one sauce and one cheese. How many cheeses are there?
questions.hint: Write 3 × 4 × c = 72 and solve for c.
questions.explanation: 3 × 4 × c = 12c = 72, so c = 6 cheeses.

questions.q: Yousef is choosing a laptop: 5 brands, each with 2 models, and each model has some memory sizes. He counts 60 different options. How many memory sizes are there for each model?
questions.hint: Multiply the known numbers and divide 60 by the result.
questions.explanation: 5 × 2 × m = 10m = 60, so m = 6. Subtracting (60 − 5 − 2 = 53) does not use the counting principle.

questions.q: Each row shows the number of choices in three categories and the total number of combinations. Fill in the missing number.
questions.hint: Total = A × B × C, so a missing factor = total ÷ product of the other two.

questions.q: For a trip, Mona packs 5 blouses, 3 pairs of trousers, 2 jackets and 4 pairs of shoes. If an outfit uses one item of each type, how many outfits can she make?
questions.hint: Multiply the number of choices for each type.
questions.explanation: 5 × 3 × 2 × 4 = 120 outfits. Adding the numbers gives 14, which is not the number of combinations.

questions.q: A school uniform shop sells 4 shirts, 3 pairs of trousers, 2 ties and 5 pairs of socks. How many different uniforms with one of each item are possible?
questions.hint: Use the Fundamental Counting Principle.
questions.explanation: 4 × 3 × 2 × 5 = 120 uniforms.

questions.q: Match each wardrobe to the number of outfits (one of each item).
questions.hint: Multiply all the numbers in each wardrobe.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a red king? Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Count the cards that are both red and kings.
questions.explanation: There are 2 red kings (hearts and diamonds), so P = 2/52 = 1/26.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard deck. What is the probability that it is a face card and a spade? (Face cards are J, Q, K.)
questions.hint: Each suit has 3 face cards.
questions.explanation: The jack, queen and king of spades are the only cards that are both, so P = 3/52.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Match each event to its probability.
questions.hint: Count the cards that satisfy both conditions at the same time.
questions.explanation: Black queens: 2/52 = 1/26. Hearts 2–10: 9/52. Clubs are black, so red and a club is impossible: 0. Ace of diamonds: 1/52.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a club or a king? Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Add the probabilities, then subtract the card counted twice.
questions.explanation: P = 13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13 (the king of clubs is counted in both groups).

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard deck. What is the probability of drawing a red card or a face card (J, Q, K)?
questions.hint: There are 6 red face cards that would be counted twice.
questions.explanation: P = 26/52 + 12/52 − 6/52 = 32/52 = 8/13. Forgetting to subtract the overlap gives 38/52 = 19/26.

questions.q: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Complete the table for P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Give counts out of 52.
questions.hint: Cards in A or B = A + B − both.
questions.explanation: Spade or ace: 13 + 4 − 1 = 16. Black or 5: 26 + 4 − 2 = 28. Ace or king: no card is both, so 4 + 4 − 0 = 8.

questions.q: One card is selected from a standard deck. Which expression equals the probability of NOT selecting a heart?
questions.hint: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
questions.explanation: There are 13 hearts, so P(heart) = 13/52 and P(not heart) = 1 − 13/52 = 39/52 = 3/4.

questions.q: One card is selected from a standard deck. What is the probability of NOT selecting a face card (J, Q, K)? Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: There are 12 face cards.

questions.q: One card is selected from a standard deck. Match each event to its probability.
questions.hint: Find the probability of the event, then subtract from 1.

questions.q: A survey found that 85% of students at a school travel by bus. If one student is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student does not travel by bus? Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: The two events are complements, so their probabilities add to 1.

questions.q: The weather forecast gives a 35% chance of rain tomorrow. What is the probability that it does NOT rain?
questions.hint: P(not rain) = 1 − P(rain).
questions.explanation: 1 − 0.35 = 0.65, so there is a 65% chance of no rain.

questions.q: Complete the table of complementary probabilities. Write each missing value as a decimal.
questions.hint: P(event) + P(not event) = 1.

questions.q: Which statement is always true for any two events A and B?
options: A ∪ B and A ∩ B always contain the same outcomes.
Every outcome in A ∪ B is also in B.
Every outcome in A ∩ B is also in A.
Every outcome in A is also in A ∩ B.
questions.hint: A ∩ B holds only the outcomes that are in both A and B.
questions.explanation: An outcome in A ∩ B is in both A and B, so it is certainly in A. An outcome of A may not be in B, so it need not be in A ∩ B. Likewise an outcome of A ∪ B may be only in A, so it need not be in B.

questions.q: A number from 1 to 8 is chosen. A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}. Complete the table with the number of outcomes in each event.
questions.hint: The intersection keeps shared outcomes; the union keeps every outcome that is in either set.
questions.explanation: A ∩ B = {3, 4}, which has 2 outcomes. A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, which has 6 outcomes. Check: n(A ∪ B) = 4 + 4 − 2 = 6.

questions.q: Match each statement about events A and B to how often it is true.

left: If x is in A ∩ B, then x is in A ∪ B.
If x is in A ∪ B, then x is in A ∩ B.
A ∩ B has more outcomes than A ∪ B.
If x is in B, then x is in A ∪ B.

questions.hint: Think of A ∩ B as 'in both' and A ∪ B as 'in at least one'.
questions.explanation: Anything in both sets or in B is in at least one set, so those are always true. An outcome in A ∪ B is in A ∩ B only when it belongs to both sets, so that is sometimes true. A ∩ B is always contained in A ∪ B, so it can never have more outcomes.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. Let A be rolling a number less than 4 and B be rolling an odd number. Find A ∩ B.
questions.hint: List A and B, then keep only the numbers in both lists.
questions.explanation: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {1, 3, 5}. The numbers in both are 1 and 3, so A ∩ B = {1, 3}. The set {1, 2, 3, 5} is the union, not the intersection.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. Let A be rolling a number greater than 2 and B be rolling a multiple of 3. Find A ∩ B. Write the set, e.g. {1, 2}.
questions.hint: Write out A and B first.
questions.explanation: A = {3, 4, 5, 6} and B = {3, 6}. Both 3 and 6 are in A, so A ∩ B = {3, 6}.

questions.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 10 is spun. A = spinning an even number and B = spinning a number greater than 6. Complete the table. Write sets like {1, 2} and probabilities as fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: Intersection: in both lists; union: in either list, each number written once.
questions.explanation: The even numbers greater than 6 are 8 and 10, so A ∩ B = {8, 10} and P = 2/10 = 1/5. Combining both lists gives A ∪ B = {2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}, with 7 outcomes, so P = 7/10.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. Let A be rolling a prime number and B be rolling an even number. What is P(A ∩ B)?
questions.hint: Find which numbers are both prime and even.
questions.explanation: A = {2, 3, 5} and B = {2, 4, 6}. Only 2 is in both, so A ∩ B = {2} and P(A ∩ B) = 1/6. The value 5/6 is P(A ∪ B).

questions.q: Which expression could be used to find 7P2?
questions.hint: nPr = n!/(n − r)!.
questions.explanation: 7P2 = 7!/(7 − 2)! = 7!/5! = 7 · 6 = 42. The expression 7!/(2!·5!) is 7C2, which counts combinations.

questions.q: Match each expression to an equivalent factorial form.
questions.hint: Use nPr = n!/(n − r)! and nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), with 0! = 1.

questions.q: Evaluate 9P3.
questions.hint: 9P3 = 9!/6!, which is the product of 3 factors starting at 9.

questions.q: Complete the table of permutations nPr.
questions.hint: nPr multiplies r numbers counting down from n.

questions.q: Hessa has 12 songs on a playlist. She will play 4 different songs, one after another. How many different orders of 4 songs are possible?
questions.hint: Order matters, so use 12P4.
questions.explanation: Order matters, so use 12P4 = 12!/8! = 12 · 11 · 10 · 9 = 11,880. There are 12 choices for the first song, 11 for the second, 10 for the third and 9 for the fourth.

questions.q: Laila has 8 videos saved and has time to watch 3 different ones, one after another. Complete the count of possible viewing orders.
questions.hint: Each video watched leaves one fewer to choose from.
questions.explanation: There are 8 choices first, then 7, then 6. By the counting principle the total is 8 · 7 · 6 = 336, which is 8P3.

questions.q: A radio host has 9 songs and will play 3 different ones in a row. How many different orders are possible?
questions.hint: The order of the songs matters and no song repeats.
questions.explanation: Use 9P3 = 9 · 8 · 7 = 504. 84 is 9C3, which ignores order, and 729 = 9³ would allow a song to be repeated.

questions.q: Match each situation to the counting method it needs.

left: Awarding 1st, 2nd and 3rd place in a race
Making a 4-digit PIN with no repeated digits
Picking 5 students to form a committee

questions.hint: Ask: if I rearrange the same items, do I get a different result?
questions.explanation: Toppings and committee members are just a group, so order does not matter: combination. Race places and PIN digits give a different result when rearranged, so order matters: permutation.

questions.q: Which situation should be counted with a combination?
options: Choosing 2 of 10 books to take on holiday
Electing a president and a vice-president
questions.hint: A combination is used when order does not matter.
questions.explanation: Taking books on holiday only depends on which 2 books you pick, so it is a combination. Shelf positions, named offices and code positions all depend on order, so they are permutations.

questions.q: Type permutation or combination for each situation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Choosing 4 cards to form a hand:

questions.hint: If swapping two items creates a different outcome, order matters.
questions.explanation: Seat numbers and rankings change when people or films are swapped, so they are permutations. A hand of cards is the same hand in any order, so it is a combination.

questions.q: Of the 10 people at a meeting, 3 will be chosen to form a team. How many different teams are possible?
questions.hint: A team is a group, so order does not matter.

questions.q: A coach chooses 5 of 8 players to start a basketball game. Positions do not matter. How many groups of starters are possible?
questions.hint: Order does not matter, so use 8C5.
questions.explanation: 8C5 = 8!/(5!·3!) = (8 · 7 · 6)/(3 · 2 · 1) = 56. The value 6720 is 8P5, which wrongly counts order.

questions.q: Complete the table of combinations nCr.
questions.hint: nCr = nPr ÷ r!.

questions.q: A club has 11 members.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Number of ways to choose 2 members as delegates:

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Number of ways to choose 9 members to stay behind:

questions.hint: Choosing who goes is the same as choosing who stays.
questions.explanation: 11C2 = (11 · 10)/2 = 55. Choosing 9 to stay behind leaves the same 2 to go, so 11C9 = 11C2 = 55.

questions.q: The digits 1 through 9 are used to make a 3-digit code. Digits cannot be repeated. What is the probability that the code uses the digits 2, 5 and 7 in any order?
questions.hint: Count all codes, then count the orders of 2, 5 and 7.
questions.explanation: There are 9 · 8 · 7 = 504 codes. The digits 2, 5 and 7 can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways. P = 6/504 = 1/84.

questions.q: The letters A to H are used to make a 2-letter code with no repeated letter. What is the probability that the code uses the letters B and E in either order? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Total codes = 8P2; B and E can appear in 2 orders.
questions.explanation: There are 8 · 7 = 56 codes. BE and EB are the 2 favourable codes, so P = 2/56 = 1/28.

questions.q: The digits 0 to 9 are used to make a 4-digit code with no repeated digits.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Codes that use 1, 2, 3 and 4 in any order:

questions.hint: Total = 10P4; the four given digits can be arranged in 4! ways.
questions.explanation: Total = 10 · 9 · 8 · 7 = 5040. The digits 1, 2, 3, 4 can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways. P = 24/5040 = 1/210.

questions.q: Five letter tiles L, E, V, E, L are placed in a bag and drawn one at a time without replacement. What is the probability that they come out in order to spell LEVEL?
questions.hint: Either L can come first, and either E can be in an E position.
questions.explanation: There are 5! = 120 orders of the tiles. The two L's can swap and the two E's can swap, giving 2! · 2! = 4 orders that spell LEVEL. P = 4/120 = 1/30.

questions.q: Six letter tiles B, A, N, A, N, A are drawn one at a time without replacement. What is the probability that they are drawn in order to spell BANANA? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Divide the number of ways to arrange the repeated letters by 6!.
questions.explanation: There are 6! = 720 orders. The three A's can be arranged 3! = 6 ways and the two N's 2! = 2 ways, so 12 orders spell BANANA. P = 12/720 = 1/60.

questions.q: Each word's letter tiles are put in a bag and drawn one at a time without replacement. Complete the table. 'Favourable orders' is the number of draw orders that spell the word. Give probabilities as fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: Favourable orders = product of the factorials of the repeated-letter counts; total orders = (number of tiles)!.
questions.explanation: MOM: the two M's can swap, so 2 of 3! = 6 orders work, P = 1/3. BOOK: 2 of 24 orders, P = 1/12. LETTER has two E's and two T's, so 2! · 2! = 4 of 720 orders work, P = 1/180.

questions.q: A code is 2 capital letters followed by 2 digits. A letter or digit cannot be used twice. What is the probability that a randomly made code is AB57? Write the answer as 1/n.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of choices for each position.
questions.explanation: Letters: 26 · 25 = 650 ways. Digits: 10 · 9 = 90 ways. Total codes = 650 · 90 = 58,500, and only one is AB57, so P = 1/58,500.

questions.q: A password is 2 lowercase letters (no repeat), then 1 symbol from @ # & *, then 1 digit.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Number of ways to choose the 2 letters:

questions.hint: Use the counting principle position by position.
questions.explanation: Letters: 26 · 25 = 650. Then 4 symbols and 10 digits: 650 · 4 · 10 = 26,000 passwords. One specific password has probability 1/26,000.

questions.q: A locker code is 3 digits with no repeated digit, followed by one letter from A, B, C, D, E. What is the probability that a random code is 482C?
questions.hint: Count the digit part with 10 · 9 · 8.
questions.explanation: Digits: 10 · 9 · 8 = 720 ways; letters: 5 ways. Total = 720 · 5 = 3600, so P = 1/3600. 1/5000 would allow digits to repeat.

questions.q: Four of 12 classmates will be chosen to help at a school event. Order does not matter.
questions.hint: When order does not matter use nCr.
questions.explanation: Order does not matter, so use a combination. 12C4 = (12 · 11 · 10 · 9)/(4 · 3 · 2 · 1) = 11880/24 = 495.

questions.q: Three of 20 students will be chosen as president, vice-president and secretary. How many ways can this be done?
questions.hint: The roles are different, so order matters.
questions.explanation: Use 20P3 = 20 · 19 · 18 = 6840. 1140 = 20C3 ignores the different roles, and 8000 = 20³ allows the same student to take more than one role.

questions.q: A class has 10 students. Match each task to its number of ways.

left: Award gold, silver and bronze to 3 students
Choose a captain and a vice-captain
Choose 2 students to clean the board

questions.hint: Use combinations for groups and permutations for different roles or positions.
questions.explanation: Committee: 10C3 = 120. Medals: 10P3 = 720. Captain and vice-captain: 10P2 = 90. Two cleaners: 10C2 = 45.

questions.q: Two students from a class of 60 will win free tickets. What is the probability that both Ahmed and his brother win? Write the answer as 1/n.
questions.hint: Count all possible pairs with 60C2.
questions.explanation: There are 60C2 = (60 · 59)/2 = 1770 possible pairs of winners. Only one pair is Ahmed and his brother, so P = 1/1770.

questions.q: Two of 30 students will be chosen at random to visit a museum. What is the probability that Mariam and Noor are the two chosen?
questions.hint: The two chosen students form a group, so order does not matter.
questions.explanation: There are 30C2 = (30 · 29)/2 = 435 possible pairs, and one of them is Mariam and Noor, so P = 1/435. 1/870 uses 30P2, which counts each pair twice.

questions.q: Three of 25 students will be chosen at random to join a trip.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Probability that 3 particular friends are chosen:

questions.hint: Use 25C3 for the number of groups.
questions.explanation: 25C3 = (25 · 24 · 23)/(3 · 2 · 1) = 13800/6 = 2300. Exactly one of those groups is the 3 friends, so P = 1/2300.

questions.q: A café offers 8 flavours. Reem picks 3 different flavours at random. What is the probability that she picks mint, mango and pistachio?
questions.hint: The order of the flavours does not matter.
questions.explanation: There are 8C3 = (8 · 7 · 6)/6 = 56 sets of 3 flavours, so P = 1/56. 1/336 uses 8P3 and counts each set 6 times.

questions.q: A pizza shop has 9 toppings. Two different toppings are chosen at random. What is the probability that they are cheese and olives? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Count the pairs of toppings with 9C2.
questions.explanation: 9C2 = (9 · 8)/2 = 36 pairs of toppings, and only one is cheese and olives, so P = 1/36.

questions.q: Three different flavours are chosen at random from n flavours. Complete the table for the number of possible sets and the probability of getting one particular set.
questions.hint: nC3 = n(n − 1)(n − 2)/6, and the probability is 1 ÷ nC3.
questions.explanation: 6C3 = 120/6 = 20, 7C3 = 210/6 = 35 and 10C3 = 720/6 = 120. Each probability is 1 over the number of sets: 1/10, 1/20, 1/35, 1/120.

questions.q: You have 5 books: Math, Art, Science, Arabic and Music. You choose 3 at random and arrange them on a shelf. What is the probability that Math is first and Art is second from the left? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Total arrangements = 5P3; fix the first two places and count the third.
questions.explanation: Total = 5 · 4 · 3 = 60. With Math and Art fixed, the third place can be any of the other 3 books. P = 3/60 = 1/20.

questions.q: From 7 different books, 3 are chosen at random and arranged in a row. What is the probability that a particular book, Biology, is first in the row?
questions.hint: Fix Biology first, then fill the other two places.
questions.explanation: Total = 7P3 = 210. With Biology first, the other places can be filled 6 · 5 = 30 ways. P = 30/210 = 1/7. 3/7 is the probability Biology is somewhere in the row.

questions.q: From 8 different textbooks, 3 are chosen at random and arranged on a shelf.
questions.hint: Once two places are fixed, only the third place is free.
questions.explanation: Total = 8P3 = 8 · 7 · 6 = 336. With History and Physics fixed, 6 books can go third. P = 6/336 = 1/56.

questions.q: Match each pair of events to independent or dependent.

left: Drawing two cards from a deck without replacement
Rolling a die and spinning a spinner
Choosing a class president, then a vice-president from the same class

questions.hint: Ask whether the first outcome changes the chances for the second.
questions.explanation: Coin flips, dice and spinners do not affect each other, so those are independent. Removing a card or a person changes what is left for the second choice, so those are dependent.

questions.q: Which pair of events is dependent?
options: Picking a sock from a drawer, keeping it, then picking another
Drawing a card, replacing it, then drawing again
Flipping a coin and rolling a die
questions.hint: Look for a choice that is not put back.
questions.explanation: Keeping the first sock changes the socks left in the drawer, so the second pick depends on the first. In the other options nothing is removed, so the events are independent.

questions.q: Type independent or dependent for each pair of events.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Draw a marble, put it back, draw again:

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Choose 2 students one after another for 2 jobs:

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Today's weather and the result of a coin toss:

questions.hint: With replacement, nothing changes between the two events.
questions.explanation: Replacing the marble restores the bag, so the draws are independent. The second student is chosen from those left, so that is dependent. The weather has no effect on a coin, so those are independent.

questions.q: A bag has 5 red and 7 blue marbles. Two marbles are taken without replacement. Which expression gives P(red, red)?
questions.hint: After the first red is taken, both the reds and the total go down by 1.
questions.explanation: First draw: 5 red of 12. Then 4 red remain among 11 marbles. P(red, red) = 5/12 × 4/11. 5/12 × 5/12 would be with replacement.

questions.q: A bag holds 3 lemons and 5 oranges. Two fruits are taken one after the other without replacement. Complete the table. Give fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: The second fraction has denominator 7 because one fruit is gone.
questions.explanation: Lemon, lemon: 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28. Orange, orange: after an orange, 4 of 7 are oranges, so 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14. Lemon, orange: after a lemon, 5 of 7 are oranges, so 3/8 × 5/7 = 15/56.

questions.q: A box has 6 apples and 4 pears. Two pieces of fruit are taken without replacement. What is P(pear, pear)? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Multiply 4/10 by the chance of a pear from the 9 fruits left.

questions.q: A bag has 15 marbles: 6 red, 5 green and 4 blue. Two are selected without replacement. What is the probability that both are green?
questions.explanation: P = 5/15 × 4/14 = 20/210 = 2/21. 1/9 = (5/15)² is the answer with replacement.

questions.q: A jar has 18 marbles: 10 red, 5 green and 3 blue. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of red first and then blue? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: After a red is removed, 17 marbles remain and all 3 blue are still there.

questions.q: A bag has 4 red and 8 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. Give fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: Same colour means red-red or blue-blue, so add those two probabilities.

questions.q: A purse has 4 one-dirham coins (AED 1), 6 fifty-fils coins and 10 twenty-five-fils coins. Two coins are grabbed at random. Round to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Use 'not' = 1 − P(event), and remember the coins are not replaced.

questions.q: A drawer has 6 black and 4 white socks. Two socks are taken at random. What is the probability that they are NOT both white?
questions.hint: Find P(both white) first, then subtract from 1.
questions.explanation: P(both white) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15. So P(not both white) = 1 − 2/15 = 13/15. 21/25 = 1 − (4/10)² wrongly assumes replacement.

questions.q: A box has 25 pens: 5 blue and 20 black. Two pens are taken at random. What is the probability that both are blue? Round to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Multiply 5/25 by 4/24.

questions.q: A pouch has 3 gold, 2 silver and 5 bronze coins. Two coins are taken at random. Complete the table with fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: There are 10 coins at first and 9 after one is taken.

questions.q: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Which pair of events is mutually exclusive?
options: Drawing an ace or a diamond
Drawing a face card or a club
Drawing a king or a red card
Drawing a heart or a spade
questions.hint: Mutually exclusive events have no card in common.
questions.explanation: No card is both a heart and a spade, so those events are mutually exclusive. The king of hearts is a king and red, the jack of clubs is a face card and a club, and the ace of diamonds is both an ace and a diamond.

questions.q: One card is drawn from a standard deck. Match each pair of events to the correct description.

left: A club or a black card
A heart or a black card

questions.hint: Try to find one card that fits both events.
questions.explanation: No card is both a queen and a king, and no heart is black, so those pairs are mutually exclusive. The 7 of hearts is red and a 7, and every club is black, so those pairs are not mutually exclusive.

questions.q: One card is drawn from a standard deck. Type true or false for each statement.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Drawing a 5 or a heart is mutually exclusive.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Drawing a diamond or a club is mutually exclusive.

questions.hint: If two events share an outcome, it must be subtracted once when adding.
questions.explanation: The 5 of hearts is both a 5 and a heart, so (a) is false. No card is both a diamond and a club, so (b) is true. The black jacks are counted twice in (c); the correct value is 4/52 + 26/52 − 2/52.

questions.q: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is P(jack or black card)? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Subtract the black jacks, which are counted twice.
questions.explanation: P = 4/52 + 26/52 − 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13. The jack of clubs and jack of spades are in both events.

questions.q: A number from 1 to 50 is chosen. Match each question to whether its two events are mutually exclusive.

left: Is it odd or a multiple of 5?
Is it a multiple of 10 or odd?
Is it greater than 40 or less than 10?
Is it a perfect square or even?

questions.hint: Look for a single number that answers yes to both parts.
questions.explanation: A number cannot be both 12 and 15, multiples of 10 are even, and no number is both above 40 and below 10, so those are mutually exclusive. 5 is odd and a multiple of 5, and 4 is a square and even, so those pairs are not mutually exclusive.

questions.q: A number from 1 to 100 is chosen. Which pair of events is NOT mutually exclusive?
options: It is a multiple of 5 or a multiple of 7
It is odd or a multiple of 8
It is less than 10 or greater than 90
It is prime or a multiple of 6
questions.hint: Find a pair that shares at least one number.
questions.explanation: 35 is a multiple of both 5 and 7, so those events overlap. Multiples of 6 are never prime, multiples of 8 are even, and no number is below 10 and above 90.

questions.q: A number from 1 to 30 is chosen. Type mutually exclusive or not mutually exclusive where asked.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Smallest number in both events of (a):

questions.hint: A common multiple of 4 and 6 is a multiple of their LCM.
questions.explanation: The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, so 12 (and 24) is in both events: not mutually exclusive. Every multiple of 4 is even, so no number is both odd and a multiple of 4: mutually exclusive.

questions.q: A random whole number from 1 to 20 is generated. What is the probability that it is a multiple of 3 or a multiple of 4?
questions.hint: Subtract the numbers that are multiples of both.
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3: 6 numbers. Multiples of 4: 5 numbers. Only 12 is in both. P = (6 + 5 − 1)/20 = 10/20 = 50%. 55% forgets to subtract 12.

questions.q: A random whole number from 1 to 15 is chosen. What is the probability that it is even or a multiple of 5? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Count evens and multiples of 5, then subtract the overlap.
questions.explanation: Even: 7 numbers. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15. 10 is in both. P = (7 + 3 − 1)/15 = 9/15 = 3/5.

questions.q: A number from 1 to 12 is chosen at random. Complete the table. Give probabilities as fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: Use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, which is 4 outcomes. Both: 6 and 12, so 2 outcomes and P = 1/6. Either: 6 + 4 − 2 = 8 outcomes, P = 8/12 = 2/3.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. The probability of a sum of 8, given that at least one die shows an odd number, is 2/27. Why is the numerator 2?
options: 8 is even, so it splits into 2 odd numbers
Only (3, 5) and (5, 3) give a sum of 8 with an odd die
questions.hint: List the pairs that sum to 8 and keep those with an odd die.
questions.explanation: Pairs summing to 8 are (2, 6), (6, 2), (3, 5), (5, 3) and (4, 4). Only (3, 5) and (5, 3) have an odd die, so 2 of the 27 outcomes work.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that at least one die shows an odd number, what is the probability that the sum is 4? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: There are 27 outcomes with at least one odd die.
questions.explanation: Pairs with sum 4: (1, 3), (3, 1), (2, 2). Only (1, 3) and (3, 1) have an odd die. P = 2/27.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled and at least one shows an odd number (27 outcomes). Complete the table. Give probabilities as fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: List each pair with that sum and check that at least one number is odd.
questions.explanation: Sum 6: (1, 5), (5, 1), (3, 3), so 3/27 = 1/9. Sum 7: all 6 pairs have an odd die, so 6/27 = 2/9. Sum 10: only (5, 5), so 1/27.

questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled (36 outcomes).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outcomes where both dice are even:

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outcomes where at least one die is odd:

questions.hint: Use the complement: at least one odd = not both even.
questions.explanation: Each die has 3 even faces, so both even happens 3 · 3 = 9 ways. The rest, 36 − 9 = 27 outcomes, have at least one odd die.

questions.q: Each of 30 students has a different number from 1 to 30. What is the probability that Omar has 25, given that he has an odd number? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Restrict the sample space to the odd numbers.
questions.explanation: There are 15 odd numbers from 1 to 30, and 25 is one of them. P(25 | odd) = 1/15.

questions.q: Each of 40 students has a different number from 1 to 40. Given that a student has an even number, what is the probability that it is a multiple of 10?
questions.hint: Count the even numbers and the multiples of 10 among them.
questions.explanation: There are 20 even numbers. The multiples of 10 are 10, 20, 30 and 40, all even. P = 4/20 = 1/5. 1/10 divides by all 40 numbers instead of the 20 even ones.

questions.q: Each of 24 students has a different number from 1 to 24. Give fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: The condition becomes the new sample space.
questions.explanation: There are 8 multiples of 3 up to 24, so P(12 | multiple of 3) = 1/8. There are 12 even numbers, and 6, 12, 18, 24 are multiples of 6, so P = 4/12 = 1/3.

questions.q: A club has caps to give away: red 8, blue 12, black 20. Caps are given away one at a time at random. What is the probability that the first two are both red?
questions.hint: Total = 40 caps; multiply 8/40 by 7/39.
questions.explanation: P = 8/40 × 7/39 = 56/1560 ≈ 0.036, or about 4%. 20% is only the first draw, and 38% comes from adding instead of multiplying.

questions.q: Caps for a tournament: white 6, grey 9, navy 15 (30 caps). Two caps are given away at random. Complete the table with fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: Multiply (colour/30) by (colour − 1)/29.

questions.q: There are 14 red and 6 green scarves. Two scarves are given away at random. What is the probability that both are red? Give a percent to the nearest whole number.
questions.hint: Multiply 14/20 by 13/19.

questions.q: Ms. Huda writes 5 names on slips: Reem, Lina, Sara, Dana and Hind. She draws two without replacement. What is the probability she draws Sara, then Reem?
questions.hint: First draw 1 of 5, then 1 of the 4 left.
questions.explanation: P = 1/5 × 1/4 = 1/20 = 5%. 4% = 1/25 would be with replacement, and 10% = 1/10 counts both orders.

questions.q: Six names are in a hat. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that Yousef is drawn first and Khalid second? Give a fraction.
questions.hint: Multiply 1/6 by 1/5.
questions.explanation: P = 1/6 × 1/5 = 1/30, because after Yousef is drawn 5 names remain.

questions.q: Four names, Amal, Bushra, Dalia and Fatma, are in a bag. Two are drawn. Give fractions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: P(Bushra and Amal in either order), without replacement:

questions.hint: Without replacement the second denominator is 3; either order doubles the chance.
questions.explanation: Without replacement: 1/4 × 1/3 = 1/12. With replacement: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Either order: 1/12 + 1/12 = 1/6.

questions.q: In a survey of 500 people, 240 live in villas. Of the 400 people who exercise weekly, 150 live in villas. What is the probability that a person exercises weekly, given that they live in a villa? Give a percent to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: Divide by the number of villa residents.

questions.q: A survey of 800 students found that 450 take the bus. Of the 520 students who eat breakfast, 270 take the bus. What is P(eats breakfast | takes the bus)?
questions.hint: The condition 'takes the bus' gives the denominator.

questions.q: In a survey of 600 people, 400 live in apartments and 200 live in villas. 450 people live with others, and 280 of them live in apartments. Complete the two-way table.
questions.hint: Each row and column must add up to its total.
questions.explanation: Apartment, alone: 400 − 280 = 120. Villa, with others: 450 − 280 = 170. Villa, alone: 200 − 170 = 30. Total alone: 600 − 450 = 150.

questions.q: Use the survey of 600 people: 400 live in apartments, 450 live with others, and 280 live in apartments with others. Give percents to the nearest tenth.
questions.hint: The 'given' group is the denominator.
questions.explanation: P(with others | apartment) = 280/400 = 70%. P(apartment | with others) = 280/450 ≈ 0.622 = 62.2%.

questions.q: A class of 30 receives the numbers 1 to 30 at random. Odd numbers join the blue team. If a student is on the blue team, what is the probability that the number is 5, 9 or 13?
questions.hint: The blue team has 15 numbers.
questions.explanation: Blue team: the 15 odd numbers. 5, 9 and 13 are 3 of them. P = 3/15 = 1/5. 1/10 = 3/30 uses the whole class.

questions.q: A class of 20 receives the numbers 1 to 20. Even numbers form the red team. If a student is on the red team, what is the probability that the number is 4 or 16? Give a fraction in simplest form.
questions.hint: Count the even numbers from 1 to 20.
questions.explanation: The red team has 10 even numbers, and 4 and 16 are two of them. P = 2/10 = 1/5.

questions.q: A class of 36 receives the numbers 1 to 36. Students with multiples of 3 form the green team.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Number of students on the green team:

questions.hint: Multiples of 3 up to 36: 36 ÷ 3.
questions.explanation: There are 36 ÷ 3 = 12 multiples of 3. 9, 18 and 27 are 3 of them, so P = 3/12 = 1/4.

questions.q: In a survey of 2000 people, 900 own a cat, and 360 of the cat owners also own a dog. A total of 750 people own a dog. What is P(owns a cat | owns a dog)? Give a decimal.
questions.hint: Divide the number with both by the number of dog owners.

questions.q: In a study of 1500 people, 600 have children, and 240 of those drive a sedan. A total of 800 people drive a sedan. What is P(has children | drives a sedan)?
questions.hint: The condition is driving a sedan.

questions.q: Of 1000 students, 400 play a sport, 300 play an instrument, and 120 do both. Match each probability to its value.
questions.hint: For a conditional, divide by the size of the given group.

questions.q: At a school, P(art and music) = 0.18 and P(music) = 0.6. What is the probability that a student takes art, given that the student takes music?
questions.hint: P(art | music) = P(art and music)/P(music).

questions.q: P(A and B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A | B)?
questions.hint: Divide, don't multiply.
questions.explanation: P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B) = 0.12/0.4 = 0.3. 0.048 comes from multiplying 0.12 × 0.4.

questions.q: Use P(B | A) = P(A and B)/P(A) to complete the table.
questions.hint: Rearrange: P(A) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B | A) and P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A).

questions.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 10 is spun. Find the probability that the number is 9, given that it is odd. Give a fraction.
questions.hint: List the odd numbers from 1 to 10.
questions.explanation: The odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, which is 5 outcomes. One of them is 9, so P = 1/5.

questions.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 16 is spun. Given that the number is even, what is the probability that it is greater than 12?
questions.hint: There are 8 even numbers; count those greater than 12.
questions.explanation: The even numbers are 2, 4, …, 16 (8 outcomes). 14 and 16 are greater than 12, so P = 2/8 = 1/4.

questions.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 12 is spun. Complete the table of conditional probabilities. Give fractions in simplest form.
questions.hint: Count only the outcomes that satisfy the condition.
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, so P(9) = 1/4. Greater than 8: 9, 10, 11, 12, two even, so 1/2. Primes: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, four odd, so 4/5.

questions.q: At a school lunch, 70% of students order juice, 42% order juice and a sandwich, and 60% order a sandwich.
questions.hint: Independent means P(sandwich | juice) = P(sandwich).
questions.explanation: P(sandwich | juice) = 0.42/0.70 = 0.6. This equals P(sandwich) = 0.6 (equivalently 0.7 × 0.6 = 0.42), so the events are independent.

questions.q: At a café, 40% of customers order coffee, 30% order coffee and cake, and 50% order cake. Which statement is correct?
questions.hint: Divide P(coffee and cake) by P(coffee), then compare with P(cake).
questions.explanation: P(cake | coffee) = 0.30/0.40 = 0.75. Since 0.75 ≠ P(cake) = 0.5, the events are not independent. 0.6 = 0.3/0.5 is P(coffee | cake).

questions.q: Complete the table. Type yes or no for 'Independent?'.
questions.hint: A and B are independent when P(B | A) = P(B).
questions.explanation: P(B | A) = P(A and B)/P(A): 0.2/0.5 = 0.4, 0.2/0.8 = 0.25, 0.3/0.6 = 0.5, 0.2/0.25 = 0.8. Compare with P(B): rows 1 and 3 match (independent); rows 2 and 4 do not.

questions.q: A Venn diagram shows the clubs chosen by a group of students. Regions: Art only 25, Music only 40, Sports only 90, Art and Music only 12, Art and Sports only 6, Music and Sports only 15, all three 7, none of the clubs 55. Give probabilities as fractions in simplest form.

parts.label: i
parts.prompt: How many students are in the group?

parts.label: ii
parts.prompt: How many students are in Music?

questions.hint: Add every region for the total, and for 'or' count each region only once.
questions.explanation: Total = 25 + 40 + 90 + 12 + 6 + 15 + 7 + 55 = 250. Music = 40 + 12 + 15 + 7 = 74. Art or Sports covers every region except Music only and none: 25 + 12 + 6 + 7 + 90 + 15 = 155, so P = 155/250 = 31/50. Only Art and Music = 12, so P = 12/250 = 6/125.

questions.q: In a Venn diagram of 120 students: Maths club only 20, Science only 30, Robotics only 18, Maths and Science only 10, Maths and Robotics only 5, Science and Robotics only 8, all three 4, none 25. A student is chosen at random. What is P(Science or Robotics)?
questions.hint: Count each region inside the Science circle or the Robotics circle exactly once.
questions.explanation: The regions inside Science or Robotics are 30 + 18 + 10 + 5 + 8 + 4 = 75. So P = 75/120 = 5/8. Adding the two circle totals (52 + 35 = 87) double-counts the shared regions.

questions.q: A Venn diagram of 100 people shows three events A, B and C: A only 14, B only 22, C only 30, A and B only 6, A and C only 4, B and C only 9, all three 3, none 12. Complete the table.
questions.hint: A circle's total is its 'only' region plus every overlap inside it.

questions.q: A survey of 200 students: Grade 10 — 30 walk to school, 70 take the bus (total 100); Grade 11 — 50 walk, 50 take the bus (total 100); totals 80 walk, 120 bus, 200 overall. Complete the relative frequency table (as percentages of the grand total).
questions.hint: Divide every count by the grand total, 200.

questions.q: A frequency table of 250 teenagers: Boys — 60 play a sport, 65 do not (125); Girls — 45 play a sport, 80 do not (125); totals 105 play, 145 do not. In the relative frequency table (percent of the grand total), what replaces the 45?
questions.hint: A joint relative frequency uses the grand total as the denominator.
questions.explanation: 45 ÷ 250 = 0.18 = 18%. Dividing by the row total 125 gives 36% and by the column total 105 gives about 43%, which are conditional frequencies, not joint ones.

questions.q: In a survey of 400 people, 92 are under 30 and prefer tea. When the frequency table is changed to a relative frequency table (percent of the grand total), what percent replaces 92?
questions.hint: Divide the cell count by the grand total.
questions.explanation: 92 ÷ 400 = 0.23, so the cell becomes 23%.

questions.q: A survey of 150 shoppers: Juniors — 36 shop online, 24 in store (60); Seniors — 54 online, 36 in store (90); totals 90 online, 60 in store.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Percent of all shoppers who are juniors and shop online (%):

questions.hint: Compare P(A and B) with P(A) × P(B).
questions.explanation: P(junior and online) = 36/150 = 24%. P(junior) = 60/150 = 0.4 and P(online) = 90/150 = 0.6, so the product is 0.24 = 24%. They are equal, so the events are independent.

questions.q: A table of 100 people: Women — 30 prefer coffee, 20 prefer tea (50); Men — 45 coffee, 5 tea (50); totals 75 coffee, 25 tea. Are 'woman' and 'prefers coffee' independent?
questions.hint: Events are independent only when P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
questions.explanation: P(woman and coffee) = 30/100 = 0.30. P(woman) × P(coffee) = 0.5 × 0.75 = 0.375. Since 0.30 ≠ 0.375, the events are dependent.

questions.q: A table of 200 people: Under 20 — 18 prefer cycling, 42 prefer running (60); 20 or older — 72 cycling, 68 running (140); totals 90 cycling, 110 running. Match each description to its percent of all 200 people.
questions.hint: Divide each count by 200.

questions.q: A survey of 210 people: City — 45 own a bike, 75 do not (120); Village — 58 own a bike, 32 do not (90); totals 103 own, 107 do not. To the nearest whole percent, what is the probability that a randomly chosen person lives in a village and does not own a bike?
questions.hint: Use the one cell for 'village and no bike' over the grand total.
questions.explanation: P = 32/210 ≈ 0.152, which is 15% to the nearest percent.

questions.q: Using the same survey (City: 45 bike, 75 no bike; Village: 58 bike, 32 no bike; total 210), what is the probability, to the nearest percent, that a random person lives in the city and owns a bike?
questions.hint: 'And' means one cell divided by the grand total.
questions.explanation: P = 45/210 ≈ 0.214 = 21%. 38% (45/120) and 44% (45/103) divide by a row or column total instead, and 57% is P(city).

questions.q: A gym recorded 250 visits: Morning — 40 used weights, 60 did not (100); Evening — 85 used weights, 65 did not (150); totals 125 and 125. Complete the joint relative frequency table as whole percents.
questions.hint: Divide each count by 250.

questions.q: A relative frequency table: Under 18 — plays guitar 0.12, does not 0.38 (total 0.50); 18 or older — plays 0.18, does not 0.32 (total 0.50); column totals 0.30 and 0.70. The probability that someone is under 18 given that they play guitar is x/0.30. Which number replaces x?
questions.hint: The numerator is the joint probability of both events.
questions.explanation: P(under 18 | guitar) = P(under 18 and guitar) ÷ P(guitar) = 0.12/0.30. So x = 0.12 and the probability is 0.4.

questions.q: Using the table (Under 18: guitar 0.12, no guitar 0.38, total 0.50; 18 or older: guitar 0.18, no guitar 0.32, total 0.50), find P(plays guitar | 18 or older) as a decimal.
questions.hint: Divide the joint value by the row total for 18 or older.

questions.q: A relative frequency table: Male — drives 0.28, does not 0.17 (0.45); Female — drives 0.33, does not 0.22 (0.55); totals 0.61 drive, 0.39 do not. P(drives | female) = numerator ÷ denominator.
questions.hint: Condition on 'female', so divide by the female row total.
questions.explanation: The numerator is P(drives and female) = 0.33 and the denominator is P(female) = 0.55. 0.33 ÷ 0.55 = 0.6.

questions.q: A survey of 160 students on favourite sport: Grade 9 — football 34, basketball 22, tennis 14 (70); Grade 10 — football 36, basketball 30, tennis 24 (90); totals 70, 52, 38. Give answers as fractions in simplest form.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Relative frequency of Grade 10 and (football or tennis):

questions.hint: Add the counts for the event, then divide by 160.
questions.explanation: Grade 10 and football or tennis = 36 + 24 = 60, so 60/160 = 3/8. Grade 9 total = 70, so 70/160 = 7/16.

questions.q: Using the same survey (Grade 9: football 34, basketball 22, tennis 14; Grade 10: football 36, basketball 30, tennis 24; total 160), what is the relative frequency of choosing basketball?
questions.hint: Use the basketball column total over the grand total.
questions.explanation: Basketball total = 22 + 30 = 52, so 52/160 = 13/40. 11/80 uses only Grade 9 and 1/3 divides by the Grade 10 total.

questions.q: 200 people were surveyed about eye colour: Green 50, Brown 80, Blue 70. Complete the relative frequency column as decimals.
questions.hint: Relative frequency = frequency ÷ total.
questions.explanation: 50/200 = 0.25, 80/200 = 0.40, 70/200 = 0.35, and the relative frequencies add to 1.

questions.q: Which is the set-builder notation for {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, …}?
questions.hint: The list contains only integers and starts at −3.
questions.explanation: The elements are the integers −3, −2, −1, … with −3 included, so x ≥ −3 and x ∈ ℤ. ℝ would include fractions, > would drop −3, and ℕ has no negatives.

questions.q: Match each set with its set-builder notation.
questions.hint: Decide which number set is used and whether the endpoint is included.
questions.explanation: Positive even numbers are 2n for n = 1, 2, 3, …. x ≥ 7 includes 7 and all reals above. {…, 0, 1, 2} is the integers up to 2. Multiples of 3 are 3n for any integer n.

questions.q: Complete each set-builder notation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Real numbers greater than −5: {x | x ___ −5, x ∈ ℝ}. Type the symbol.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: All multiples of 7: {x | x = ___n, n ∈ ℤ}

questions.hint: Read each description carefully: 'greater than' excludes the endpoint.
questions.explanation: Greater than −5 uses >. The list starts at 10 and contains integers, so x ≥ 10. Multiples of 7 are 7n for integers n.

questions.q: Write each set of numbers in interval notation.
questions.hint: Use [ ] for ≤ and ≥, ( ) for < and >, and always ( ) next to ∞.
questions.explanation: −1 ≤ x ≤ 6 includes both ends: [−1, 6]. x ≥ 2 is [2, ∞). 0 < x ≤ 3 is (0, 3]. The 'or' statement is a union: (−∞, −1) ∪ [4, ∞).

questions.q: Match each inequality with its interval notation.
questions.hint: Check whether each endpoint is included.
questions.explanation: Strict < on both sides gives (−5, 2). x ≥ −5 is [−5, ∞). −5 ≤ x < 2 is [−5, 2). x < 2 is (−∞, 2).

questions.q: Which interval notation represents x ≤ −3 or x > 1?
questions.hint: 'Or' joins two pieces with a union.
questions.explanation: x ≤ −3 includes −3: (−∞, −3]. x > 1 excludes 1: (1, ∞). 'Or' means union, so (−∞, −3] ∪ (1, ∞).

questions.q: Given h(x) = x² − 5x + 2, find each expression in expanded form.
questions.hint: Replace every x in h with the new input and simplify.

questions.q: Given f(x) = 2x² − 3x + 1, find f(x − 2).
questions.hint: Expand 2(x − 2)² carefully and distribute −3 over (x − 2).

questions.q: Given k(x) = x² + 4x − 1, complete the table.
questions.hint: Substitute each x-value, squaring negative numbers inside brackets.

questions.q: Given g(x) = x² + 6x, find g(−x) in simplest form.
questions.hint: (−x)² = x².

questions.q: State the domain of f(x) = (x − 2)/(x² + 5x).
questions.hint: Factor the denominator and set it equal to zero.
questions.explanation: x² + 5x = x(x + 5) = 0 when x = 0 or x = −5. Those values are excluded; the numerator does not matter.

questions.q: For f(x) = (x + 1)/(x² − 9), list the x-values excluded from the domain.
questions.hint: x² − 9 is a difference of squares.
questions.explanation: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), which is zero at x = −3 and x = 3. So the domain is all reals except ±3.

questions.q: Match each function with the values excluded from its domain.
questions.hint: Find where each denominator equals zero.
questions.explanation: x(x − 4) = 0 at 0 and 4. (x − 2)(x + 2) = 0 at ±2. (x + 3)² = 0 only at −3. x² + 1 is never zero, so nothing is excluded.

questions.q: Decide whether each relation represents y as a function of x.
questions.hint: A function gives exactly one y for each x.
questions.explanation: y = 3x² − 1 gives one y per x. x = y² + 2 gives y = ±√(x − 2), two values. In the first set no x repeats (repeated y is fine). In the last set x = 2 has two y-values.

questions.q: Which relation does NOT represent y as a function of x?
questions.hint: Try solving for y and see if you get ± .
questions.explanation: x² + y² = 9 gives y = ±√(9 − x²), so x = 0 pairs with y = 3 and y = −3; it fails the vertical line test. The others give one y per x.

questions.q: Complete the table: is y a function of x? Type yes or no.
questions.hint: Imagine a vertical line moving across each graph.
questions.explanation: y = x³ − 4 gives one y per x. y² = x + 1 gives y = ±√(x + 1). x = 5 is a vertical line, so x = 5 has infinitely many y-values. y = 7 is a horizontal line, which is a function.

questions.q: State the domain of each function in interval notation.
questions.hint: A radicand must be ≥ 0, and > 0 if the root is in a denominator.
questions.explanation: 2x − 6 ≥ 0 gives x ≥ 3. 9 − x² ≥ 0 gives −3 ≤ x ≤ 3. x + 2 > 0 (strict, because of the denominator) gives x > −2.

questions.q: What is the domain of f(x) = √(x² − 16)?
questions.hint: Solve x² − 16 ≥ 0.
questions.explanation: x² ≥ 16 means x ≤ −4 or x ≥ 4. The endpoints are included because √0 = 0 is defined.

questions.q: State the domain of f(x) = 1/√(x² − 1) in interval notation.
questions.hint: The radicand must be strictly positive here.
questions.explanation: We need x² − 1 > 0, so x² > 1, giving x < −1 or x > 1. The endpoints are excluded because they would make the denominator 0.

questions.q: Match each function with its domain.
questions.hint: Set each radicand ≥ 0 (or > 0 in a denominator).
questions.explanation: x + 5 ≥ 0 gives x ≥ −5. 5 − x ≥ 0 gives x ≤ 5. x − 5 > 0 gives x > 5. 25 − x² ≥ 0 gives −5 ≤ x ≤ 5.

questions.q: Let f(x) = 4 if x < −2; f(x) = x² − 1 if −2 ≤ x ≤ 3; f(x) = 3/x + 1 if x > 3. Find each value.
questions.hint: First decide which condition each x-value satisfies.

questions.q: Let g(x) = 2x + 1 if x < 0; g(x) = √(x + 4) if 0 ≤ x ≤ 5; g(x) = 10 − x if x > 5. Find g(5).
questions.hint: x = 5 belongs to the piece whose condition includes 5.
questions.explanation: 5 satisfies 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, so g(5) = √(5 + 4) = √9 = 3. Using 10 − x would wrongly give 5.

questions.q: Let g(x) = 2x + 1 if x < 0; g(x) = √(x + 4) if 0 ≤ x ≤ 5; g(x) = 10 − x if x > 5. Complete the table.
questions.hint: Choose the piece by the condition, then substitute.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x + 3 if x < 0 and f(x) = 2 if x ≥ 0. Plot the points of the graph at x = −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2.
questions.hint: Use the first rule only for negative x.
questions.explanation: f(−2) = 1 and f(−1) = 2 from x + 3. For x ≥ 0 the value is always 2: (0, 2), (1, 2), (2, 2).

questions.q: Find the zeros of f(x) = 2x² − 7x + 3.
questions.hint: Factor into two binomials.
questions.explanation: 2x² − 7x + 3 = (2x − 1)(x − 3). Setting each factor to zero gives x = 1/2 and x = 3.

questions.q: For f(x) = x² − 2x − 8, plot both x-intercepts, the y-intercept and the vertex.
questions.hint: Factor to find the zeros; the vertex is halfway between them.
questions.explanation: x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2), so the zeros are −2 and 4. f(0) = −8. The vertex is at x = 1 and f(1) = 1 − 2 − 8 = −9.

questions.q: What are the zeros of f(x) = 3x² + 5x − 2?
questions.hint: Look for factors (3x + a)(x + b).
questions.explanation: 3x² + 5x − 2 = (3x − 1)(x + 2). So 3x − 1 = 0 gives x = 1/3 and x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2.

questions.q: A function's graph starts at a closed dot at (−4, 2), falls to a minimum at (−1, −3), then rises to an open circle at (3, 5). Find the domain and range.
questions.hint: Open circles exclude that value; check whether the y-value is reached elsewhere.
questions.explanation: x runs from −4 (included) to 3 (excluded): [−4, 3). The lowest y is −3, and y gets close to 5 but 5 is never reached, so the range is [−3, 5).

questions.q: A graph starts at an open circle at (−2, 1), rises to a maximum at (1, 6), then falls to a closed dot at (4, −2). What are its domain and range?
questions.hint: Read x from left to right, y from lowest to highest.
questions.explanation: x goes from −2 (open) to 4 (closed): (−2, 4]. The lowest y is −2 at the closed dot and the highest is 6, so the range is [−2, 6].

questions.q: Each graph is a single straight segment. Complete the domain and range in interval notation.
questions.hint: An open endpoint removes both its x-value and its y-value.
questions.explanation: Segment 1 includes both ends: domain [−2, 3], range [−1, 4]. Segment 2 excludes (0, 5): domain (0, 6], range [−1, 5).

questions.q: Match each function with its type.
questions.hint: Compute f(−x) and compare with f(x) and −f(x).
questions.explanation: x⁵ − 2x³ has only odd powers, so f(−x) = −f(x): odd. 2x⁴ − x² + 7 has only even powers and a constant: even. x² + x mixes even and odd powers: neither. |−x| = |x|, so |x| + x² is even.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x³ − 4x.
questions.hint: Replace x with −x.
questions.explanation: f(−x) = (−x)³ − 4(−x) = −x³ + 4x = −(x³ − 4x) = −f(x), so f is odd.

questions.q: The function f(x) = x⁶ − 2x² + 3 is:
questions.hint: Check f(−x).
questions.explanation: f(−x) = (−x)⁶ − 2(−x)² + 3 = x⁶ − 2x² + 3 = f(x), so f is even; its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.

questions.q: Test y = x² − 4 for symmetry. Answer yes or no.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Symmetric with respect to the x-axis?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Symmetric with respect to the y-axis?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Symmetric with respect to the origin?

questions.hint: Replace x with −x, y with −y, or both.
questions.explanation: x → −x gives y = x² − 4, unchanged: y-axis symmetry. y → −y gives −y = x² − 4, different, so no x-axis symmetry. Both gives −y = x² − 4, different, so no origin symmetry.

questions.q: The graph of xy = 6 is symmetric with respect to:
questions.hint: Try (−x, −y), (x, −y) and (−x, y).
questions.explanation: (−x)(−y) = xy = 6, so it is symmetric about the origin. x(−y) = −xy and (−x)y = −xy, which give −6, so there is no axis symmetry.

questions.q: The graph of x = y² − 3 is symmetric about the x-axis. Plot the points on it with y = 2, 1, 0, −1 and −2.
questions.hint: Substitute each y-value to get x.
questions.explanation: y = ±2 gives x = 1, y = ±1 gives x = −2, and y = 0 gives x = −3. The points come in mirror pairs (x, y) and (x, −y), confirming x-axis symmetry.

questions.q: Match each equation with its symmetry.
questions.hint: Test each replacement: x → −x, y → −y, and both.
questions.explanation: y = x³ is unchanged only when both signs flip: origin. y = x⁴ + 1 is unchanged by x → −x: y-axis. x = y⁴ − 2 is unchanged by y → −y: x-axis. x² + y² = 16 is unchanged by all three.

questions.q: Which of the following functions is/are odd? I. f(x) = x⁴ − x   II. f(x) = x³ + 5x   III. f(x) = −2x⁵
questions.hint: An odd function satisfies f(−x) = −f(x).
questions.explanation: I: f(−x) = x⁴ + x, which is neither f(x) nor −f(x). II: f(−x) = −x³ − 5x = −f(x), odd. III: f(−x) = 2x⁵ = −f(x), odd.

questions.q: Which of the following functions is/are even? I. f(x) = x² − 6   II. f(x) = x³ + x²   III. f(x) = 4 − x⁴
questions.hint: An even function satisfies f(−x) = f(x).
questions.explanation: I: (−x)² − 6 = x² − 6, even. II: −x³ + x² ≠ f(x), not even. III: 4 − (−x)⁴ = 4 − x⁴, even.

questions.q: Complete the table: find f(−x) and classify each function as even, odd or neither.
questions.hint: Replace x with −x; odd powers change sign, even powers do not.
questions.explanation: (−x)³ − 2(−x) = −x³ + 2x = −f(x): odd. (−x)² + 4 = x² + 4 = f(x): even. (−x)² − 3(−x) + 4 = x² + 3x + 4, which is neither f(x) nor −f(x): neither.

questions.q: The graph of h is made of line segments joining (−5, −2), (−3, 2), (1, −2) and (3, 0) in order. The point (−5, −2) is an open circle and (3, 0) is a closed dot.
questions.hint: Find where each segment crosses the x-axis; use the segment's equation to read values.
questions.explanation: Segment (−5, −2)→(−3, 2) has slope 2 and crosses at x = −4. Segment (−3, 2)→(1, −2) is y = −x − 1: zero at −1, h(−2) = 1, y-intercept −1. The last segment reaches 0 at x = 3. Domain (−5, 3]; y = −2 is reached at (1, −2), so the range is [−2, 2].

questions.q: A function's graph is made of line segments joining (−4, 2), (−2, −2), (1, −2) and (3, 2). Plot all of its x-intercepts and its y-intercept.
questions.hint: Find where each segment crosses y = 0, and the value at x = 0.
questions.explanation: From (−4, 2) to (−2, −2) the slope is −2, so y = 0 halfway, at x = −3. From (1, −2) to (3, 2) y = 0 at x = 2. The flat segment at y = −2 passes x = 0, so the y-intercept is (0, −2).

questions.q: A graph starts at a closed dot at (−3, 4), falls to (0, −2), then rises to an open circle at (2, 3). What is its range?
questions.hint: The highest y-value is at the closed starting dot.
questions.explanation: The lowest point is (0, −2) and the highest is the closed dot (−3, 4). The open circle at y = 3 does not matter since y = 3 is reached elsewhere. Range: [−2, 4]. ([−3, 2) is the domain.)

questions.q: Analyze f(x) = ∛(x − 1).
questions.hint: Cube roots of negative numbers exist.
questions.explanation: ∛(x − 1) = 0 when x = 1. f(9) = ∛8 = 2. Any real number has a cube root, so the domain is all reals. f(0) = ∛(−1) = −1.

questions.q: Complete the table for f(x) = ∛x + 2.
Plot the points of y = ∛x at x = −8, −1, 0, 1 and 8.
questions.hint: Find the cube root of each x-value.

questions.q: Which statement about f(x) = ∛x is true?
options: Its domain is [0, ∞) and its range is all real numbers.
Its domain and range are both [0, ∞).
Its domain and range are both all real numbers.
questions.hint: Unlike a square root, a cube root accepts negative inputs.
questions.explanation: ∛x is defined for every real x and takes every real value (negative, zero and positive). Its zero is x = 0.

questions.q: A graph starts at a closed dot at (−5, 0), rises to a maximum at (−2, 4), falls to a minimum at (2, −3), then rises to an open circle at (4, 1). Find the domain and range.
questions.hint: Use the endpoints for the domain and the max and min for the range.
questions.explanation: x runs from −5 (closed) to 4 (open): [−5, 4). The lowest y is −3 and the highest is 4, both reached, so the range is [−3, 4].

questions.q: A graph is a straight segment from an open circle at (−1, −2) to a closed dot at (5, 6). What are its domain and range?
questions.hint: The open circle excludes both x = −1 and y = −2.
questions.explanation: The segment includes x-values just above −1 up to 5, so (−1, 5]. Its y-values go from just above −2 up to 6, so (−2, 6].

questions.q: Match each graph with its domain.

left: ray from closed (−2, 1) going right forever

questions.hint: Closed dot → bracket, open circle → parenthesis.
