questions.hint: Isolate cos θ.
questions.explanation: 2 cos θ = 2, so cos θ = 1. This happens at θ = 0 and every full turn after, so θ = 2kπ.

questions.q: In the interval 0° ≤ x < 360°, how many values of x satisfy cos²x = 3/4?
questions.hint: Take square roots: remember ±.
questions.explanation: cos x = √3/2 gives 30° and 330°; cos x = −√3/2 gives 150° and 210°. That is 4 values.

questions.q: Solve tan²x = 1 for 0° ≤ x < 360°.
questions.hint: tan x = 1 or tan x = −1.
questions.explanation: tan x = 1 gives 45° and 225°; tan x = −1 gives 135° and 315°. There are 4 solutions, from 45° up to 315°.

questions.q: In the interval 0° ≤ x < 360°, how many values of x satisfy sin²x = 1?
questions.hint: sin x = 1 or sin x = −1; each happens once per turn.
questions.explanation: sin x = 1 at 90° and sin x = −1 at 270°. That is 2 values.

questions.q: For 0° ≤ x < 360°, complete the number of solutions of each equation.
questions.hint: Take ± square roots, then count angles for each value.

questions.q: Solve 5 cos x = 3 cos x + √3 (k is any integer).
questions.hint: Collect the cos x terms on one side.
questions.explanation: 2 cos x = √3, so cos x = √3/2. In one turn this happens at π/6 and 11π/6. Adding full turns gives x = π/6 + 2kπ or x = 11π/6 + 2kπ.

questions.q: Solve 4 tan²x − 1 = 3 for all x (k is any integer). Write the answer as one family.
questions.hint: tan²x = 1, so tan x = ±1.
questions.explanation: 4 tan²x = 4, so tan²x = 1 and tan x = ±1. The solutions π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4 are spaced π/2 apart, so x = π/4 + kπ/2.

questions.q: Solve 4 cos²x − 3 = 0 for all x (k is any integer).
options: x = π/3 + kπ or x = 2π/3 + kπ
x = π/6 + kπ or x = 5π/6 + kπ
questions.hint: cos²x = 3/4 gives two values of cos x.
questions.explanation: cos x = ±√3/2. cos x = √3/2 gives π/6, 11π/6 and cos x = −√3/2 gives 5π/6, 7π/6. π/6 and 7π/6 are π apart, as are 5π/6 and 11π/6, so x = π/6 + kπ or x = 5π/6 + kπ.

questions.q: Solve 2 sin²x + 3 cos x − 3 = 0 on [0, 2π).
questions.hint: Replace sin²x with 1 − cos²x to get a quadratic in cos x.
questions.explanation: 2(1 − cos²x) + 3 cos x − 3 = 0 becomes 2cos²x − 3cos x + 1 = 0, so (2cos x − 1)(cos x − 1) = 0. cos x = 1/2 gives π/3 and 5π/3, and cos x = 1 gives 0. So x = 0, π/3, 5π/3.

questions.q: Find the solutions of 2cos²x + 3 sin x − 3 = 0 on [0, 2π).
questions.hint: Use cos²x = 1 − sin²x.
questions.explanation: 2 − 2sin²x + 3 sin x − 3 = 0 gives 2sin²x − 3 sin x + 1 = 0, so (2 sin x − 1)(sin x − 1) = 0. sin x = 1/2 gives π/6, 5π/6 and sin x = 1 gives π/2.

questions.q: How many solutions does 2 sin²x − cos x − 1 = 0 have on [0, 2π)?
questions.hint: Write it as a quadratic in cos x and factor.
questions.explanation: 2(1 − cos²x) − cos x − 1 = 0 gives 2cos²x + cos x − 1 = 0, so (2cos x − 1)(cos x + 1) = 0. cos x = 1/2 gives π/3, 5π/3 and cos x = −1 gives π. That is 3 solutions.

questions.q: Find the solutions of sec x − tan x = 1 on [0, 2π].
questions.hint: Write as (1 − sin x)/cos x = 1, solve, then check for undefined or extraneous values.
questions.explanation: 1 − sin x = cos x. Squaring gives 1 − 2sin x + sin²x = 1 − sin²x, so 2sin²x − 2sin x = 0 and sin x = 0 or 1. sin x = 1 makes cos x = 0 (undefined). sin x = 0 needs cos x = 1, so x = 0 and 2π; x = π fails since cos π = −1.

questions.q: Find the solution of csc x + cot x = 1 on [0, 2π].
questions.hint: Rewrite as (1 + cos x)/sin x = 1 and check each candidate.
questions.explanation: 1 + cos x = sin x. Squaring gives 2cos²x + 2cos x = 0, so cos x = 0 or −1. cos x = −1 makes sin x = 0 (undefined). cos x = 0 gives π/2 or 3π/2; checking, π/2 works (1 + 0 = 1) but 3π/2 gives 1 ≠ −1. So x = π/2.

questions.q: Solve tan x + sec x = 1 on [0, 2π].

questions.hint: Write as (sin x + 1)/cos x = 1, so sin x + 1 = cos x.
questions.explanation: Squaring sin x + 1 = cos x gives sin²x + 2sin x + 1 = 1 − sin²x, so 2sin²x + 2sin x = 0 and sin x = 0 or −1. sin x = −1 makes cos x = 0, so tan and sec are undefined. sin x = 0 needs cos x = 1, giving x = 0 and 2π (x = π is extraneous).

questions.q: When solving csc x − cot x = 1 on [0, 2π], a student finds the candidates x = 0, π/2 and 2π. Why are x = 0 and 2π rejected?
options: csc x and cot x are undefined there
questions.hint: Check where sin x = 0.
questions.explanation: At x = 0 and 2π, sin x = 0, so csc x = 1/sin x and cot x = cos x/sin x are undefined. Only x = π/2 is a valid solution.

questions.q: Solve sin θ = sin²θ for 0 ≤ θ < 2π. List the solutions from smallest to largest.
questions.hint: Move everything to one side and factor out sin θ.
questions.explanation: sin²θ − sin θ = 0 gives sin θ(sin θ − 1) = 0. sin θ = 0 gives 0 and π; sin θ = 1 gives π/2. In order: 0, π/2, π.

questions.q: Solve cos²θ = cos θ for 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
questions.hint: Factor cos θ(cos θ − 1) = 0.
questions.explanation: cos θ(cos θ − 1) = 0. cos θ = 0 gives π/2 and 3π/2; cos θ = 1 gives 0.

questions.q: How many solutions does tan²θ + tan θ = 0 have for 0 ≤ θ < 2π?
questions.hint: Factor out tan θ.
questions.explanation: tan θ(tan θ + 1) = 0. tan θ = 0 gives 0 and π; tan θ = −1 gives 3π/4 and 7π/4. That is 4 solutions.

questions.q: A student solves tan θ = tan²θ (0 ≤ θ < 2π) by dividing both sides by tan θ and gets only π/4 and 5π/4. Which solutions were lost?
questions.hint: Dividing by tan θ assumes tan θ ≠ 0.
questions.explanation: Dividing by tan θ throws away the case tan θ = 0. Factoring tan θ(tan θ − 1) = 0 instead keeps tan θ = 0, which gives θ = 0 and π.

questions.q: Solve 2 sin x cos x + sin x = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π. List the solutions from smallest to largest.
questions.hint: Factor out sin x.
questions.explanation: sin x(2cos x + 1) = 0. sin x = 0 gives 0 and π. cos x = −1/2 gives 2π/3 and 4π/3. In order: 0, 2π/3, π, 4π/3.

questions.q: Solve √2 cos x − 2 sin x cos x = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
questions.hint: Factor out cos x.
questions.explanation: cos x(√2 − 2 sin x) = 0. cos x = 0 gives π/2, 3π/2. sin x = √2/2 gives π/4, 3π/4. All four are solutions.

questions.q: Solve 2 sin x cos x − sin x = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π by completing the table. List solutions smallest first, separated by a comma.
questions.hint: Factor sin x(2cos x − 1) = 0.
questions.explanation: sin x = 0 gives x = 0 and π. 2cos x − 1 = 0 gives cos x = 1/2, so x = π/3 and 5π/3.

questions.q: How many solutions does tan x sin x − sin x = 0 have for 0 ≤ x < 2π?
questions.hint: Factor out sin x.
questions.explanation: sin x(tan x − 1) = 0. sin x = 0 gives 0 and π (tan x is defined there). tan x = 1 gives π/4 and 5π/4. That is 4 solutions.

questions.q: Solve 2cos²x + sin x − 1 = 0 on [0, 2π). List the solutions from smallest to largest.
questions.hint: Replace cos²x with 1 − sin²x and factor.
questions.explanation: 2 − 2sin²x + sin x − 1 = 0 gives 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0, so (2 sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0. sin x = 1 gives π/2 and sin x = −1/2 gives 7π/6 and 11π/6.

questions.q: Which equation is obtained when 2cos²x − 3 sin x = 0 is rewritten in terms of sin x only?
questions.hint: Substitute cos²x = 1 − sin²x and multiply by −1.
questions.explanation: 2(1 − sin²x) − 3 sin x = 0 gives 2 − 2sin²x − 3 sin x = 0. Multiplying by −1: 2sin²x + 3 sin x − 2 = 0.

questions.q: The equation 2sin²x + 3 sin x − 2 = 0 factors as (2 sin x − 1)(sin x + 2) = 0. Complete the table for 0 ≤ x < 2π (write 'none' if there is no solution; list solutions smallest first).
questions.hint: Sine values must lie between −1 and 1.
questions.explanation: sin x = 1/2 is possible and gives x = π/6 and 5π/6. sin x = −2 is impossible because −1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1, so it gives no solutions.

questions.q: f(x) = x² for x < 2, f(2) = 1, and f(x) = 6 − x for x > 2. Find each value (write DNE if it does not exist).
questions.hint: Limits use the pieces near x = 2; f(2) uses only the value at x = 2.
questions.explanation: From the left, x² → 4. From the right, 6 − x → 4. Both sides agree, so the limit is 4. The function value is defined separately as f(2) = 1.

questions.q: g(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≤ 1 and g(x) = x² − 4 for x > 1. Find lim x→1 g(x).
questions.hint: Compare the left-hand and right-hand limits.
questions.explanation: From the left, 2(1) + 1 = 3. From the right, 1² − 4 = −3. The one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist.

questions.q: f(x) = x + 2 for x < 0, f(0) = 5, f(x) = x² + 2 for 0 < x < 3, and f(x) = 8 for x ≥ 3. Complete the table (write DNE if a limit does not exist).
questions.hint: Use the piece to the left of a for the left-hand limit and the piece to the right for the right-hand limit.
questions.explanation: At 0: x + 2 → 2 and x² + 2 → 2, so the limit is 2, while f(0) = 5. At 3: x² + 2 → 11 from the left and the right piece is 8. The sides differ, so the limit does not exist; f(3) = 8 since x ≥ 3 includes 3.

questions.q: A graph of f has an open circle at (3, 1) and a filled dot at (3, 4). The curve approaches the point (3, 1) from both sides. Find each value (write DNE if it does not exist).
questions.hint: The limit follows the curve; the function value is the filled dot.
questions.explanation: Both sides of the curve head toward height 1, so the one-sided limits and the limit are all 1. The filled dot shows the actual value f(3) = 4.

questions.q: f(x) = 3 − x for x ≤ −1, f(x) = x² for −1 < x < 2, and f(x) = 1 for x ≥ 2. Find each value (write DNE if it does not exist).
questions.hint: Check which piece is used on each side and which piece includes the endpoint.
questions.explanation: At −1: 3 − (−1) = 4 from the left and (−1)² = 1 from the right, so the limit does not exist; f(−1) = 4 because x ≤ −1 includes −1. At 2: x² → 4 from the left and the constant 1 from the right.

questions.q: On a graph of f, the left branch ends at a filled dot at (2, −1) and the right branch starts at an open circle at (2, 5). Which statement is true?
questions.hint: The filled dot gives the function value; each branch gives a one-sided limit.
questions.explanation: The left branch approaches −1 and the filled dot means f(2) = −1. The right branch approaches 5, so lim x→2⁺ f(x) = 5. The one-sided limits differ, so lim x→2 f(x) does not exist.

questions.q: A graph of h is described: near x = 4 the curve approaches height 3 from both sides, with an open circle at (4, 3) and a filled dot at (4, 7). At x = −1 the left piece ends at a filled dot (−1, 2) and the right piece starts at an open circle (−1, 0). Match each item to its value.
questions.hint: Limits follow the curve; values come from filled dots.
questions.explanation: Near 4 both sides approach 3, so the limit is 3, but the filled dot gives h(4) = 7. To the right of −1 the curve approaches 0. The left side approaches 2, which differs, so lim x→−1 h(x) does not exist.

questions.q: f(x) = x³ for x < 1, f(1) = 3, and f(x) = 2x − 1 for x > 1. Find lim x→1 f(x). Write DNE if it does not exist.
questions.hint: Compute both one-sided limits; ignore f(1).
questions.explanation: From the left, 1³ = 1. From the right, 2(1) − 1 = 1. Both sides agree, so the limit is 1 (the value f(1) = 3 does not matter).

questions.q: f(x) = −x for x < 0, f(0) = 3, f(x) = x² for 0 < x ≤ 2, and f(x) = 8 − x for x > 2. Which statements are true? I. lim x→0 f(x) = 0  II. lim x→2⁻ f(x) = 4  III. lim x→2 f(x) exists
questions.hint: Compute the one-sided limits at 0 and at 2.
questions.explanation: At 0, −x → 0 and x² → 0, so I is true (f(0) = 3 does not matter). From the left of 2, x² → 4, so II is true. From the right, 8 − x → 6 ≠ 4, so the limit at 2 does not exist and III is false.

questions.q: g(x) = x + 1 for x < 1, g(1) = 5, and g(x) = 3x − 1 for x > 1. Which statements are true? I. lim x→1 g(x) = 2  II. g(1) = 2  III. lim x→1⁺ g(x) = 5
questions.hint: The limit and the function value at x = 1 can be different.
questions.explanation: From the left, 1 + 1 = 2; from the right, 3(1) − 1 = 2, so I is true. g(1) = 5, so II is false. The right-hand limit is 2, not 5, so III is false.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x for x < 3, f(3) = 9, and f(x) = x + 3 for x > 3. Write true or false for each statement.
questions.hint: Find each one-sided limit and compare with the value f(3).
questions.explanation: From the left, 2(3) = 6; from the right, 3 + 3 = 6, so the limit is 6 (I true). f(3) = 9, so II is false. The right-hand limit is 6, not 9, so III is false.
